subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TAX ON FOOD
OPPOSITION TO NEW SYSTEM OF TAXATION OF NORTHERN BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have the honour to present two petitions signed by residents of northern Manitoba. In their petition, the undersigned citizens of Canada avail themselves of their ancient and undoubted right to present a petition. In the opinion of the petitioners the new system of tax deductions for northern residents has been unfairly applied leaving out many northern communities such as Thompson and Mabowden, and that the taxing of northern benefits is heavy-handed and complicated, taxing away benefits intended to compensate employees for loss of other amenities.
The petitioners call upon the House of Commons to direct the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to reconsider the system of tax measures when studying tax reform as promised in the Budget.

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-OPPOSITION TO CORPORATE PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have two petitions. The first petition deals with the Post Office and indicates that the federal Government's proposal to seek financial self-sufficiency by 1988 for Canada Post Corporation will result in cut-backs, deterioration of service of the Post Office and consequently will be at the expense of service to Canadians. It goes on to outline this in more detail.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to instruct the Government to make improved service the highest priority of the Canada Post Corporation and to abandon its policy of closing rural post offices and cancelling rural postal routes.
I have petitions which measure approximately two inches in height, petitions which are printed on legal-sized paper. I wish to make note of the fact that we have received at least 15,000 petitions from the Province of British Columbia, as well as

subsubtopic: CANADA POST-TWICE DAILY DELIVERY IN DOWNTOWN WINNIPEG
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the second petition deals with a more local matter. It is from Winnipeg. It indicates that Canada Post Corporation plans to cut delivery of mail to businesses in downtown Winnipeg to once a day instead of maintaining the present practice of twice daily delivery. The volume of mail delivered to these businesses is on the increase. Twice daily mail delivery is needed to ensure efficient operation of the businesses in downtown Winnipeg. It is unacceptable that postal service be reduced at a time when postal rates have been increased.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to instruct the Government to insist that Canada Post Corporation continue to provide twice daily mail delivery to businesses in downtown Winnipeg.

The House resumed consideration from Friday, August 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andre:
That a Message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their Honours that this House agrees with amendment 10(a) made by the Senate to Bill C-22, An Act to amend the Patent Act and provide for certain matters in relation thereto, but disagrees with all other amendments except amendments 1(c) and 8, because this House believes that amendments 1(a) and (b), 2(a) and (b), 3, 4(a) and (b), 5(a) and (b), 6, 7(a) and (b), 9 and 10(b) and (c) are in contradiction to the principles of the Bill which will increase intellectual property protection, increase research and development in Canada, create new high-technology jobs, improve the health care of Canadians, and protect consumers from higher drug prices. More specifically:
Amendments 1(a) and (b) delete the definitions of "Board" and "patentee". These definitions are necessary to support the powers of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, which is required to protect consumers.
Amendments 2(a) and (b) reduce Canada's export potential and fine chemical manufacturing.
Amendments 3, 4(a) and (b), reduce the periods of market exclusivity, thus eliminating the incentive for increased research and development in Canada.
Amendment 5(a) reduces the period of market exclusivity and export potential, thus reducing economic benefits for Canada.
Amendment 5(b) deletes the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, which is required to protect consumers, and this amendment also removes the protection for Canadian-invented medicines and thus the incentives for increased research and development in Canada.
Amendments 6, 7(a) and (b), 10(b) and (c) arise out of amendments 1(a) and (b), 2, 3, 4(a) and (b), 5(a) and (b), and are therefore inappropriate.
Amendment 9 arises out of Senate amendment 8, but is not consistent with the House amendment to Senate amendment 8, as set out below.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday the Minister intervened with remarks regarding the amendments put forward by the Upper Chamber. I want to take a few moments today to share with you, Mr. Speaker, some of my thoughts with regard to the Minister's expressed statements, as well as his sentiments, with regard to the acceptance or lack of acceptance by Canadians concerning the formulation of Bill C-22.
It is somewhat ironic that the Minister's statements on that particular day for whatever reasons, intentional or otherwise, did not focus on the fact that six provincial Legislatures were against Bill C-22 and in favour of the amendments put forward by the Upper House. The Minister went on at length to explain that in his view countless Canadians from coast to coast were in support of Bill C-22. What the Minister failed to
August 24, 1987

do was to give a great deal of specifics to that point, and I make one example. He made reference to the fact that Dalhousie University is in support of Bill C-22. Contrary to what the Minister has told the House, we had a very reputable and distinguished Canadian from that university appear before our committee who clearly spelled out his objections to the Bill. I believe it is on the record of the committee. He made some very sincere recommendations on how to improve the Bill, how it ought to be changed. Nevertheless, the distinct impression was left by the Minister of corporate affairs that that particular university was in complete harmony with Bill C-22.
Early on in the debate, particularly at committee stage, Canadians were told by the present Minister of corporate interests that the benefits to Canadians with regard to research and development would be overwhelming, indeed. 1 am trying to paraphrase the words the Minister used but I think the gist of his thesis at that time was that all provinces and territories would benefit substantially from the promises-and I would like to underline the word "promises"-from the multinational corporations as they relate to research and development. Unfortunately, if one were to accept in a hypothetical sense their promises as being guarantees and then look at the abstract as to where the moneys would go or not go, I think Hon. Members would readily agree that the economic benefits, if those were to occur, would certainly not be spread in an equal way across the country.
I was waiting for the Minister to stand in his place as the Minister of corporate interests and tell us the number of new jobs and the amount of research that would take place in the Province of Newfoundland. 1 thought he might have a comment or two with regard to how those alleged economic benefits would help the community of Corner Brook, Newfoundland. 1 thought he might stand in his place and talk about the number of new jobs that would be created in Stephenville, Newfoundland. I thought that perhaps he might have been a little bit more explicit in telling us the plans that his friends in the multinational corporations have for erecting new companies in Goose Bay, Labrador, or in St. John's, Newfoundland. But, for whatever reasons, whether it be with respect to time or his refusal to acknowledge that no benefits, or very few, will accrue to that province, the Minister of corporate interests decided not to share with us where those benefits would go in the Province of Newfoundland.
Even better, I was hoping that the Minister, who has said many, many times that economic benefits would accrue across the country, would tell the good people of Lunenburg County, Cumberland Country, Cape Breton County, Guysborough, Halifax and Pictou Counties in Nova Scotia about those benefits and the new jobs, and how many would be created in their province. When we consider New Brunswick 1 was waiting with bated breath to hear about the number of jobs that would be created in that province. We know that because of the day of reckoning-election day-which is so imminent in the Province of New Brunswick, the Minister would want to

do something for his colleagues in that province and tell us where the research and development dollars will go, the amount of dollars and the number of jobs that will be created.
We were wondering how many jobs would be created in Westmorland-Kent and in Moncton, how many would be created around that very distinguished and prestigious university, Mount Allison University, and how many would be created in Saint John, New Brunswick and other communities throughout the province. But, again, the Minister of corporate interests was not able, or shall we say not willing, to share with the House where this new grandiose sum of money would be invested in the Province of New Brunswick.
With three elected Members of Parliament in Prince Edward Island out of a total of four we were hoping that the Minister would avail himself of the opportunity to say to the people of Atlantic Canada that there might not be much in New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, but perhaps there would be a tremendous number of economic benefits in Prince Edward Island. I checked the press releases that had gone out and I did not find that the Hon. Member from Charlottetown, or the Hon. Member for Malpeque (Mr. Gass), or the other Member of Parliament from P.E.I., had made any announcements to their constituents in terms of the benefits of research and development, jobs, and economic spin-off. Perhaps some will yet come. The Minister has previously changed his mind on certain benefits of Bill C-22, perhaps he will change it again. The Minister will not guarantee, but he will promise that perhaps something may occur.
I thought that the Minister would have availed himself of the opportunity to spell out to the people of British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba where the benefits would accrue in those provinces.
There is a great university in Brandon, Manitoba. Mr. Stanley Knowles, is the Chancellor of that university, a distinguished honourary Member of the House, and former member of the New Democratic Party. I thought that the Government would have spelled out the opportunities for their colleagues and friends in Manitoba and where the benefits would accrue in that province. There are very few, if any, benefits if one assumes that the promises would be realized, or that the promises would eventually become guarantees.
We have heard a great deal in terms of new jobs in Ontario and Quebec. I do not think that any Member begrudges those two provinces the new jobs, new wealth, and economic spinoffs that may accrue. What is disturbing is that it is a mere promise, there are no guarantees. There are no guarantees on the level of expenditure for research and development, with regard to the number of jobs or with regard to the types of jobs that may be created. We are asking the Government to put in some guarantees to legitimize some of its more grandiose sentiments, and to convince the Canadian public that what it is

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
doing for the multinational corporations will bring some economic benefits to Canadians.
The Government is giving one element of the pharmaceutical industry an extended monopoly provision for approximately 10 years. The fact is that from 1969 to 1983 the pharmaceutical industry in Canada was the most profitable of any manufacturing sector in our economy. During that period the growth in employment of the manufacturing sector was approximately 4 per cent. In the pharmaceutical industry it was 29 per cent. The pharmaceutical sector in Canada had astronomical profits in the 300 to 400 percentage range. That was operating under the old law. Now the Government wants to give the pharmaceutical sector a further 10-year period of monopoly.
There is something wrong when all that is given away, and in return Canadians only get promises of additional research and development, additional jobs, and that prices will not rise. We also get a promise from the Minister that benefits will be distributed equitably throughout the country. We also get a promise from the Minister that as a result there will be more research and development in Canada. But where are the guarantees? Are Canadians to give up a good system in return for mere promises? Surely the Minister must realize, notwithstanding his desire, tenacity, and enthusiasm to satisfy the interests of his friends in the multinational corporations, that he has a further, if not greater obligation to consumers and the public that he must have a better deal, a better package for Canadians.
This morning I raised my concern about the fact that six provincial governments are opposing and want further changes to Bill C-22. 1 had hoped that the Minister would have taken their concerns very seriously. The Minister has made repeated reference to the Province of Quebec. The Minister states that there is a resolution from the Quebec Legislature which asks that we pass Bill C-22 quickly, because it believes much research and development, and jobs will be created in that province. I have no desire to enter into a confrontation with my colleagues from Quebec, regardless of what side of the House they are on. But I say to them, through you, Sir, and to members of the Government, that we on this side of the House want to see research and development, and jobs in the Province of Quebec, but we also want to see guarantees and undertakings by those corporations that things will be done as promised, and that Canadians will not have to pay higher drug prices in return for that mere promise. That is our substantive argument with regard to Bill C-22 and how it affects the Province of Quebec.
Surely as Canadian politicians and legislators we want to ensure that Canada has the best public policy affecting pharmaceuticals. Perhaps I am wrong and there are some Members who do not want that. Perhaps Members from British Columbia do not want to have research and development in their province; perhaps they do not want to have more jobs. I do not know, but 1 do not think that. The fact remains that all of us have to be concerned with the entire national
picture. 1 would hope that our colleagues in Ontario would not expect the Province of Newfoundland, and the taxpayers of that province to pay higher drug prices for their families, their children, their senior citizens, and a variety of citizens on the mere promise and whim that at some future time in the 10-year period there may be more research and development, and jobs created elsewhere.
I think it is evident that as it now stands, the Conservative Government's public policy is shady and does not serve the best interests of Canadians. When we examine the statements of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about reconciliation and better federal-provincial relations, what better judge of the success of those goals than having six provincial Governments saying that the Government's public policy does not serve the best interests of Canadians? We must consider those representations by the provinces seriously.
Furthermore, we should consider what we heard from the Province of Saskatchewan. Initially, Saskatchewan was publicly opposed to Bill C-22. There followed a provincial election and the awarding of $1 billion for agriculture programs to that province. Then mystically, Saskatchewan came onside to support Bill C-22. I do not know what brought about that change and I am not saying that $1 billion from the federal treasury convinced Saskatchewan to support Bill C-22. Others have suggested precisely that, but I am not. However, we witnessed a totally different phenomenon at the committee hearings when we were greeted by a senior deputy minister from the Province of Saskatchewan who placed so many qualifications on Bill C-22 for it to be improved in various ways that any logical person could see that Saskatchewan was reverting back to its original position of opposing Bill C-22. Quite rightly, of course, the astute deputy minister had to announce that government policy was to support Bill C-22 but with some 11 pre-conditions in terms of changing the legislation.
Let us consider Nova Scotia. I do not use that province as one of those opposing the Bill but let us consider what happened in that case. The Minister of Health for the province stated that it would cost Nova Scotians some additional $25 million.

speechtext: It is not supposed to cost anything.

speechtext:
The Member is absolutely right. The Minister of corporate interests told us the other day that it would not cost Canadians anything. But that is not what we were told by the Tory province in Nova Scotia.
However, at approximately the same time there was talk about funding for Sysco modernization. Let me make it perfectly clear that it is not my suggestion but that of some others in Nova Scotia who say that once the Sysco modernization funds were announced there seemed to be a change of heart in the Nova Scotia Government with respect to Bill C-
August 24, 1987

22. The media had a difficult time finding people to substantiate their claim of an additional cost of $25 million. As well, the Minister of corporate interests vowed to stay away from any comments about the situation in Nova Scotia. At the same time, there was a litany of announcements ranging from money for Pictou industries to funding for a variety of programs in Halifax. 1 suggest it is quite obvious to most Canadians that a major power play was underway.
It is my belief that the new Government in British Columbia, being interested in jobs and more money for research and development, would have seen through the major omissions in Bill C-22 as did six other provinces, and perhaps Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. I thought it would want to correct those omissions in order to reap some of the benefits for its province. However, there were only a few opposition MPs, including the House Leader for the New Democratic Party, who repeatedly raised the major omissions in this Bill. Government Members of Parliament from that province sat on their hands and agreed that the most profitable sector in pharmaceutical manufacturing needed another 10-year period of monopoly.
The Minister stands in his place to talk about the overwhelming support for the Bill. If he were here in the chamber I would tell him to be more candid and specify the areas of support and the rationale for that support. I think it is clearly evident that provincial Governments definitely do not support higher drug prices.
What did the Minister do? The Minister stated from the outset, through the committee stage and during the discussions in the Upper Chamber, that the Government would provide $100 million to lessen the impact if, in fact, there were higher drug prices. Either the price of drugs will rise or they will not, but the Minister tells us that he will provide $100 million. When I asked the Minister how he arrived at that figure of $100 million, he did not have any substantive answer but simply said that it is a cushion that the Government will provide to assist the provinces if prices increase. The Minister stated that consistently from January through to the early part of August. Now the Minister of corporate interests tells us a different story. The Government will no loner provide $100 million to assist provinces vis-a-vis price increases.
The Minister echoed the words of the Right Hon. Prime Minister who condemned the Upper Chamber as a bunch of political unelected hacks. I take strong exception to that statement. Lowell Murray happens to come from my constituency in Nova Scotia and I do not think he is a political hack. I am at odds with the Right Hon. Prime Minister when he calls a native Nova Scotian like Findlay MacDonald a unelected political hack. I think it is pretty degrading for the Right Hon. Prime Minister to say that about individuals in the Upper Chamber, particularly when he does not have the intestinal fortitude to do something about this unelected Chamber other than to talk rhetoric with some of his followers during his political gatherings across the country. He does not
Patent Act
have the intestinal fortitude to change a situation that can only be changed by a Prime Minister.
Do you know what the Minister of corporate interests did, Mr. Speaker? Imagine this. He accepted recommendations made by a bunch of unelected political hacks in the Upper Chamber. After saying that they were so terrible, he has now accepted some of those recommendations.
Is he going to give $100 million to the provinces for the purposes of increasing the prices of pharmaceutical drugs? No, he is not going to do that. The Minister is so confident that the multinational corporations will do research and development that he will give $100 million to the provinces, not for the purpose of price increases but for the purpose of providing additional research and development. If there has ever been hypocrisy practised in the House of Commons by any Minister of the Crown, it has been by the Minister of corporate interests whose total concerns are escalating and enhancing the profits of multinational corporations at the expense of every-day Canadians.
It is one thing to say to the provinces, "The hell with you". That is what Bill C-22 is saying. It is another thing to say to Parliament, "We believe prices will rise, therefore we will give the provinces some money," and then turn around and do the exact opposite with that money. It is another thing to refer to the Upper Chamber, as the Prime Minister and the Minister of corporate interests have, as a bunch of political hacks but to do nothing but denounce it on national television and at every political gathering they can muster. They have said to Canadians from coast to coast that they will accept no amendments, no changes, they are in it to the end, but the Minister of corporate interests came into the House and swallowed himself completely by accepting amendments. I find that behaviour to be absolutely against the best interests of generating good public policy in Canada.
How can we believe the Minister when he says now that the multinational corporations will give x millions of dollars when in the space of six months, the Minister flip-flopped not once but twice on two major, substantive issues concerning Bill C-22 and the Upper Chamber. I am absolutely astounded that the Minister could walk into the House and still feel that he could assume his responsibilities as Minister protecting Canadian consumers. It is absolutely unbelievable.
The provinces, by and large, are against this Bill. Some are against it for different reasons, but they are against it. The Minister of corporate interests has changed the legislation substantively and is hoping that Canadians will now believe him. I do not think they will.
If there is any indication that Canadians do not believe the Minister of corporate interests, we should go back to the polls for a moment since it was the Minister, not I or my colleagues to the left, who brought up the polls. This is unfortunate because I do not think that national political Parties should be

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
overly concerned with what the polls are saying on a day-today basis. However, it was the Minister of corporate interests who brought them up. He ought to look at what Decima is telling him about the trust in both his Leader and his Party. He should find out where Gallup says that particular Party is when it comes to general acceptance by the population. Of course, other pollsters have said the same thing.
It was the Minister of corporate interests who raised the issue of polls. Canadians from coast to coast know that this Government is not a Government to be trusted, particularly with regard to Bill C-22 and how changes to the Bill will affect consumers.
Since I have already talked about the provinces, let me talk for a few moments if I may about the organizations other than Dalhousie University to which the Minister alluded as being in support of Bill C-22. The Minister said that these organizations are supportive of Bill C-22. In part, the Minister of corporate interests is correct. However, when I or my colleagues to the left asked questions of these organizations at committee stage, it became very clear to many observers that amendments ought to be sought in order to strengthen the Bill and achieve the objectives about which all three political Parties were talking, namely, jobs, research and development and protection for Canadian consumers.
I remember a distinguished group of representatives from western Canada who had indicated to the committee that they were supportive of Bill C-22. When it was brought to their attention that the Bill did not contain a definition of research, they were quite surprised. I asked them, "Did you read the Bill?" They said, "Well, yes, you know, we are not lawyers but we have examined the contents of the Bill and we think it is okay". I said, "Did you see any provisions in that Bill to guarantee that research and development by those multinational firms will take place?" They said, "No, we didn't, it wasn't there". I said, "That's right, there are no guarantees". I said, "Did you see any guarantees about the number of jobs that will be created?" They said, "No, we didn't see any of those either". I said, "What guarantees did you see in the Bill for protecting consumers and the prices they will have to pay?" They said, "Well, we really don't know what its powers are, but there is such a thing as the Patent Medicines Review Board. Is that not supposed to keep prices down?"
Many groups came before the committee with good intentions, accepting the word of the Minister of corporate interests, not consumer interests, that these objectives were contained in the Bill. Those objectives were jobs, research and development expenditures, and a pricing mechanism. Once they became aware of the major omissions, they wrote to the Minister of corporate interests saying they agree its objectives are laudable but he has an obligation to put something in the Act to guarantee Canadians that this will be done. That has never taken place.
In 1984 the Tories said they were going to do away with some boards and regulations. Now they are adding another board and putting more regulations into play. Say one thing and do the opposite. We have come to accept that sort of conduct by the governing Party.
At best the constitutionality of the price review board is in serious question. It would be interesting to send a copy of that Bill to the Canadian Bar Association meeting at the Congress Centre this week. I am sure they would come to the same conclusion I have, that it is unconstitutional. I challenged the Minister. I said if he believed it to be just and appropriate, table the legal opinion to verify it. He will not do it. You would think if someone had a strong case he would want the Canadian people and, in particular, opposition Members to see what judicial interpretation the Department of Justice and his Department are giving to that legislation.
As I said to the Minister and his legal counsel in committee, at the first opportune moment, when this board attempts to exercise its authority against the multinational corporation, it will end up in Federal Court where it will remain for months and months if not a year or two before the court renders a decision nullifying any effect this board might have.
First, it is unconstitutional. Second, the board is not in a position to act, it can only react. You know, Mr. Speaker, because you are a distinguished parliamentarian, that there is quite a distinction between acting and reacting. This board can only react after it has received complaints, or provincial Governments interfere, and then it has the responsibility to investigate. What can it investigate? It is not allowed to go outside the boarders of Canada to obtain information or evidence regarding a particular company. If your corporate head offices are in New Jersey or Switzerland all you have to do is mail your file there and the Canadian Government cannot investigate whether you are transfer pricing or whether you have given the appropriate information regarding the initial cost of a particular drug. It is an absolute and utter joke. We are not looking at days, weeks or even months, we could be looking at years in dealing with a price problem.
What has happened here is very sad. The Minister has said no to committee members; he has said no to countless witnesses; he has said no to consumer advocate groups; he has said no to provincial Governments, and he has said no to legal experts-no changes will be made. Let there be no mistake about it. He is the Minister of corporate interests. He is going to embellish and enhance multinational corporations. That is what his portfolio is all about. He told the committee one thing, to which my friend from Windsor-Walkerville will probably refer, but he tells the House something different. I want it to be known through you, sir, that I am not suggesting for one moment that he is intentionally misleading the House. What I am suggesting is that in the Minister's pronouncements he has conveniently forgotten certain specifics.
August 24, 1987

I should say at this point that a number of groups who are against Bill C-22 have also said they could live with it if certain amendments were made. I want to make it perfectly clear that the amendments put forward in committee, on the floor of this House, and in the Upper Chamber have been consistent. Given the economic framework within which the multinationals operate, we do not believe Bill C-22 as put forward by the Government should pass. We cannot support the Bill with a 10-year price protection without guarantees for research and development and quality jobs across this country.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this has been an exhausting and, at times, acrimonious debate on Bill C-22. Upon reflection, perhaps I have contributed to that acrimony. However, in all good conscience I make no apologies. Someone somewhere has to stand up for those Canadians who cannot now afford the cost of prescription drugs.
In his own testimony before the committee and in his speech in introducing this legislation the Minister said that 85 per cent of Canadians are covered by drug programs. He failed to say that those drug programs are paid for by the Canadian taxpayer. He also failed to say that over one million Canadians have no drug plan whatsoever.
Notwithstanding the tenacity of Members opposite who tried to intimidate a number of witnesses in committee, we heard a number of witnesses who came before the committee say that they are welfare recipients and that some of their drugs are paid for by the municipality which pays their welfare, but that there are a good number of drugs for which they must pay themselves.
Someone must stand up for those individuals. Someone must stand up for Canadians who do not have lobbyists, as do the banks and pharmaceutical companies. Someone must say that this law is unjust. It flies in the face of providing good public policy for Canadians, whether for the senior citizen in Nova Scotia, the person on compensation in New Brunswick or Newfoundland, or the widow or welfare recipient in Prince Edward Island, Ontario or Quebec. Regardless of who those individuals are, the Government is doing a major injustice to them all.
The Government is telling the Government of Alberta and the Government of Manitoba that it does not care, that it does not give a damn what they say, that it is going to go ahead with its plan for higher drug prices with no guarantees of research and development jobs. It is responding to the conditional approval which the Government of Saskatchewan has given to this Bill by saying that it is not going to accommodate the request of the Government of Saskatchewan. It is saying to the people of British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec that there are no guarantees of jobs or research and development, that it will go on a whim and prayer that sometime in the next ten years there will be some new jobs in research and development.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not apologize for standing up for those people. They are just as important as the lawyers, doctors, and other organizations which have paid lobbyists to act on their behalf. I want to thank you, Sir, for your cooperation and the courtesy that you have, displayed to me while you have been in the Chair. I think you know deep down that I feel very strongly about the substance of this Bill. I believe very strongly that the Government of Canada has abdicated its responsibilities to the people of Canada. More important, Mr. Speaker, I believe that on judgment day, which is not all that far away, the Canadian people will give the Government its due, and I can assure you that it will not be a vote of confidence, but will be a vote in opposition to the governing party and particularly the Right Hon. Prime Minister and the Minister of corporate interests.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that I have only 20 minutes during which to express my Party's opposition to Bill C-22. It is perhaps appropriate that we allow the Official Opposition unlimited time to develop its thoughts. It is quite evident that such a length of time is required. The previous speaker is somewhat like Beethoven attempting to finish a symphony. We never know when it is going to end.
The New Democratic Party has not found it necessary to engage in the verbal athletics, as has the Official Opposition, in order to express and manifest its support for those in the country who oppose this legislation. As you well know, Mr. Speaker, Members of the New Democratic Party tabled petition after petition from the people of this country in opposition to Bill C-22. Therefore, we do not need two days in which to indicate to the Canadian people our opposition to this legislation and the reason for our opposition to it.
Quite basically we are opposed to this legislation because it is wrong. We are opposed to it because it is unnecessary. We are opposed to it because it does not recognize the various needs which must be addressed, not only those of the multinationals but those of the old, the poor, the taxpayer, and the health system of the country.
This Bill proposes to change an arrangement which originated in 1969 and introduced compulsory licensing. At that time brand name drugs had to face competition from generic drugs which have the same pharmaceutical properties. That change in Canadian patent regime resulted in considerable savings to Canadians. Let us remind ourselves that at that time Canada had among the highest drug prices in the world. Several commissions studied the matter and reached the conclusion that the only appropriate way of dealing with the problem was

the compulsory licensing arrangement which we have had since then.
Let us also remind ourselves that since that time the multinational drug companies operating in this country have had the highest profits of any manufacturing sector in the country. During that time employment in the pharmaceutical industry increased by 29 per cent more than employment in that sector in the United States where there was complete patent protection. During all of that time and before 1969, in spite of obscene profits, the multinational pharmaceutical manufacturers did not a whit of basic research in this country. We are expected to believe that by returning to the pre-1969 situation, and by virtue of a promise, they are going to keep prices down, do research in this country, and create jobs. Anyone who believes that believes in the tooth fairy. Much more, such a one probably believes that the promises of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) will be kept. We know that that would be a peculiar set of beliefs.
I listened with great interest to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) who talked at great length about what a significant impact this legislation will have on scientific research. We heard him say as well that all scientists would back this legislation because it will produce increased research opportunities and innovations. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that as a practising scientist up until the day 1 was elected to this place, I have never heard such an nonsensical view of the real situation in this country with respect to science.
It is certainly true that government after government-and this Government is no exception-has refused to make the kind of commitment to basic research that is necessary for this country to thrive. To suggest that Bill C-22 will change that situation indicates nothing but a complete misapprehension of the real world or a deliberate attempt to mislead. The Government is trying to defend the indefensible to a country in which the vast majority of people who have addressed themselves to the issue of Bill C-22 have spoken in opposition to it.
The Minister recited a long list of those who are supposed to be unequivocally in support of Bill C-22. Let us just take a couple of examples of those the Government purports are in favour of Bill C-22. The Minister tells us that Dr. Stuart Smith of the Science Council supports the Bill, and that must be interpreted to mean that Bill C-22 is seen by Dr. Smith as the only possible approach to securing research investment in the pharmaceutical industry. But what in fact did Dr. Smith say? He said, "To summarize, Science Council members agree some research is better than none''. That is a clear reference to the fact that these companies, who have given the Minister their promise, have not been doing research to any significant degree and any improvement in that situation by whatever mechanism, whether the Eastman mechanism or the Bill C-22 mechanism, would be welcome in that context.
Dr. Smith goes on to say, "We commend the Government that intellectual property will be better protected". But there are any number of approaches to improving the protection afforded to intellectual property. One way of protecting intellectual property is to see that the originator is paid royalties. The issue then becomes, how much in royalties? One could also protect to an appropriate degree-that is, in balance to all the other demands which have to be met on behalf of the people-by affording four years of exclusivity as well as some other regime of royalty payments, as Dr. Eastman has suggested.
As Dr. Smith observes, there are some deficiencies with respect to this Bill in social costs. He states:
We have some concerns about social costs. Mostly we worry that Bill C-22 does not by itself, or with any other policy, really bring about a change and improvement in Canada's pharmaceutical industry or its international balance of payments.
Does that sound like an unequivocal endorsation of Bill C-22, Mr. Speaker? Of course, it does not. It was not Dr. Smith's intention that the Minister stand here and say that the head of the Science Council is four-square in favour of Bill C-22.
The Minister also said that the University of Manitoba supports this Bill. My colleague telephoned the University of Manitoba and, as one might expect, because there should be common sense involved in the notion that a university would support this legislation, that university did not endorse this legislation.
We could go through the entire list of those associations the Minister says support this legislation and we would find the same degree of equivocation among most of them, with the exception of the Pharmaceutical Association of Canada. Of course, it supports anything that would get these people, that is the multinational pharmaceutical industry, mostly American owned, to put more money into this country for research.
Having made reference to the long list of so-called supporters referred to by the Minister, 1 have to say that the Minister has said a great deal about the inappropriateness of the Senate's attempt to significantly amend this legislation. The position of my Party is clear. It has always been clear. The Senate, as it is presently constituted, deserves abolition. If the Government feels that the Senate should be abolished, the Prime Minister has the support of my Leader and, presumable, if they can work it out, the support of the Liberal Party. So let us get on with that. But let us not call into question what is obviously true. There is a constitutional power of the Senate to deal with this issue.
Having referred so constantly to the undemocratic nature of the other place, it has to be said that the other place accorded more opportunity for those who are opposed to this Bill to speak than did the Government. It was a shameful performance on the part of the majority members of the committee who held hearings on this legislation that witnesses who expressed themselves in opposition were badgered. Their time was limited. The Hon. Member from Burlington, in his

remarks to those who expressed themselves in opposition to this Bill, could only be regarded as a poor reflection on this House, and manifestly undemocratic in his behaviour with respect to the process. Therefore, in my opinion, we have the silly situation that we, who regard this House as the place where democracy has a voice, are in the position that it is the Senate which provides those in opposition to the bill the greatest opportunity to express themselves.
What came about was a recommendation by the Senate to amend this Bill along the lines of those recommended by the Eastman Commission. The Eastman Commission carried out the most thorough study of drug legislation in the history of this country. It is a study which is respected around the world. The Eastman Commission said there should be some change in the present arrangements, that there should be four years of exclusivity, not 10 years, and there should be a specific mechanism for ensuring that research would be done, not a namby-pamby promise on the part of an industry which, in making the promise, knows that it has joined with the Government in misleading the Canadian people about what really is afoot.
When we consider tax concessions for research, the new arrangements for matching funds between industry and NSRC for funding university research, the increasing average age of the population and therefore the increased demand for pharmaceuticals, and when we look at the projections of the increases in rates of expenditures for research over the last five or ten years, what we must conclude is that by 1995 there will be an additional $1.3 billion more spent on research, so-called, in any case, whether or not this legislation is passed. In addition to that sum there would be something in the order of $2 billion spent on additional capital expenditures. This translates into an empty promise in the sense that that promise was based on a set of facts that would have existed whether or not Bill C-22 is passed.
Let us consider the type of research that will be done. Is this investment of the kind that will establish the concerted centres of excellence in the country that will pursue basic research? My colleague, the Minister, talks a great deal about basic research. He knows nothing about basic research if he thinks that what the drug companies will do is basic research. If he wants basic research, then he should put some more money into the universities to keep the promise made by the Prime Minister that the rate of investment in research would reach 2.5 per cent of the GNP. That is how basic research is increased. There are very few companies, certainly not American, Swiss, British or German ones, with their centres in their home countries which will disperse their research efforts in Canada. It is an unreasonable proposition to make. Thus we have a mixture of complete misunderstanding of what basic research is all about, and an attempt to use what was already there as justification for what should not be.

It is a Government that could have had a well thought out proposition for protecting consumers, for stimulating a measure of research, not on the basis of a promise, but on the basis of a mechanism that would make that promise come true. But, no, it wanted to play a fast one on the Canadian people.
This is a Government that is characterized by the vast majority of Canadians as being fundamentally dishonest, lacking in credibility, in a hurry to do but slow to listen, a Government that has sold its credibility because of its own failings. It has an opportunity through a reconsideration of Bill C-22 to bring what it does into closer agreement with the will of the people.

But I guess that is not possible for a Government that takes its orders from Washington.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the new policy concerning patents happens to be one of our Government's policies which may very well prove to be one of the most beneficial to this country.
This policy has several objectives.
Patent Act
One is to turn Canada's pharmaceutical industry into a leading innovating sector through significant increases in research and development investments.
The percentage of sales invested in Canada by research and development firms has been rather low in the past, particularly when compared with that of such countries as the United Kingdom, Switzerland or the Federal Republic of Germany. In addition, prospective research investors do not particularly favour Canada because the drug industry has no guarantee with respect to the protection period it can expect to have for its patented products, something we want to rectify through this legislative measure.
Drug industry growth and competitiveness rest entirely on the discovery and development of new products, and on improving existing treatments. This is why it is imperative that it be allowed to benefit from its own research or make others benefit from it.
Low investments in Canada are a serious problem, especially when we consider that a country's economic expansion is geared to research and development. It is indeed one of the basic components of sustained economic expansion, and Hon. Members would know that industrial expansion is the cornerstone of this Government's economic recovery strategy.
The amendments to the Patent Act will change the present situation. The new policy represents a true research encouragement by widening patent protection. Bill C-22 will ensure that the pharmaceutical industry will enjoy for the medecine it has discovered an exclusivity period which is long enough to allow it to recover its research investments. The prospect of making profitable investments will certainly encourage researchers to develop new and efficient drugs which will benefit all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, the innovative firms have promised to double their investments. This commitment means that research and development over the next ten years will increase from the current 4.9 percent of sales to 10 percent. This represents an additional $1.4 billion. This will bring to $3 billion the total amount which the industry will spend in research and development activities in Canada, not only in clinical research, but also in basic research.
Employmentwise, this increased research activity will create 3,000 new jobs in Canada for our high technology graduates. Our universities, hospitals, private research establishments everywhere in Canada, not only in Quebec and in Ontario, as was suggested these past few days, but everywhere in Canada, will benefit from this increased research. It is foreseen that up to 30 percent of the amounts provided for will go to these establishments and still more significant amounts will go to regions other than Quebec and Ontario.
On the medical level, one could not overemphasize the benefits from increased research. From the beginning of this debate, highly reputable people in all spheres and especially that of science have voiced their support. Through their

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
representations, Mr. Speaker, these medical authorities are not seeking monetary benefits. They are concerned, through their research, with discovering new drugs to improve the quality of life for Canadians. In the January 13 issue of the Le Devoir newspaper, Dr. Morin, a famous Quebec cardiologist, was reported as saying:
Beyond the principle of protecting intellectual property rights, the 1969 ordinance caused irreparable damage. Twenty years ago, Montreal was one of the major medical centres of the pharmaceutical industry. We have tried the utmost to chase it away.
When he appeared before the Legislative Committee, Dr. Michel Chretien stated, and I quote:
One of the major openings for these students entering the field of biomedical research is the pharmaceutical industry. However, this industry has had to limit its research staff, again because of the 1969 legislation. Young people have every reason to be concerned and reluctant. ..
to enter this field of study.
Dr. Chretien pointed out that, of the hundred or so who have graduated of the Montreal Clinical Research Institute since 1967, none now works in the Canadian pharmaceutical industry. Four of them hold important positions in France, in Switzerland and in Germany, but not here. Dr. Chretien closed by saying that, as a biomedical scientist, he is in favour of amending the Patent Act to provide new stimulus to pharmaceutical research and make our industry internationally competitive.
Then, Mr. Gagne, from the University of Montreal, pointed out that opponents of the bill have never mentioned the months of hospitalization which could be avoided thanks to better drugs.
Mr. Speaker, the health of all Canadians will be improved, and this means that the costs incurred by our health system will be significantly reduced. The more we delay passage of this Bill, the more the benefits from this piece of legislation will be long in coming. Canadians will be the ones to suffer, particularly because the development of new and more effective treatment will be delayed.
Many reservations have been expressed about whether or not the innovative industry will respect its commitments for research and development. I can assure the House that this policy will result in an unprecedented increase of research expenditures.
The innovative industry has already provided concrete evidence of its good faith. Several companies have already announced publicly, even before passage of this Bill, investments amounting to over $700 million. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that the promised amounts will be invested only after the bill is adopted.
The expenditures involved will affect fundamental research as well as clinical research and facility development. Here are three examples:
-$132.9 million will be spent over the next ten years in Alberta research centres, universities and hospitals;
-the Terry Fox Foundation and the Wellcome Foundation Ltd. will finance a biotechnical research centre at a cost of $40 million;
-the Upjohn Company in Toronto will provide $30 million for biotechnical research over the next five years and spend $22 million on capital projects.
I want to emphasize that innovative firms have no incentive whatsoever not to honour those commitments. They have everything to lose, starting with their reputations. Once their reputations are tarnished, it would be almost impossible to regain the public's and the Government's confidence.
In conclusion, I would like to say a few words on the mechanisms chosen by this Government to ensure that innovative firms honour their commitments. First, there is the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board which must submit to Parliament a yearly report including the percentage of research and development expenditures versus sales figures, not only for the overall innovative industry but also for each of its member firms. This is a most powerful tool which will inform us regularly on the performance of individual, innovative firms.
The legislation also provides for two formal reviews of the policy, to ensure that it serves the interests of Canadians. The first review will be made by Cabinet at any time after the expiration of four years after the Act comes into force. Parliament will make the second review, after the expiration of nine years after the Act has come into force. On those two occasions the Government will therefore be in a position to reduce or abolish the protection period if innovative firms have not met their commitments.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I do not understand the position taken by the Opposition on the Bill. On the one hand, the New Democratic Party is trying to sow fear and concern among seniors and the ill, when we know that group is completely covered by health-care programs. During their awareness campaigns directed to those people, they took this opportunity to fill their Party's coffers. On the other hand, strangely enough, they did not try to do the same thing in Quebec, because in Quebec the Senior Citizen's Federation along with a number of other agencies-and that Federation has over 200,000 members-support the Bill. As far as the Official Opposition is concerned, there is really nothing to understand. After repeated pressures at the time from the pharmaceutical industry-that was after 1969 and until 1980-the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Hon. Andre Ouellet, launched a process to review the act. The Liberal Party, if it were consistent with itself and its ideology, should support Bill C-22. If they do not support the legislation, they will show once more they do not know what they are doing and on many issues have no set policies.

I think that from the minute the Bill is implemented, the next day those millions and billions of dollars will be announced. So I do not see why we would not trust an industry that used to be prosperous in Canada, that was chased away because of the 1969 Act and that is now preparing to announce a $1-billion investment effort, and above all the creation of so many new jobs for our young scientists and researchers.

subsubtopic: STUDENTS' ENTITLEMENT TO POST-SECONDARY EDUCATION ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hundreds of native Indian students acquired Indian status under Bill C-31, passed by this House two years ago. Those students are entitled to post-secondary education assistance from the Department of Indian Affairs. However, they have been told they may not be able to go to school next month after all. There is no more funding for them at this time, although they are being told efforts are under way to obtain the necessary funds. They are being told to wait until Ottawa makes a decision. In the meantime they are in limbo.
They cannot leave their home communities to look for apartments because they do not know if they will receive funding. They risk losing their places in the courses in which they have enrolled. They cannot wait any longer.
They must know now whether they can go to school and they need the answer immediately. Therefore I urge the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) to end this uncertainty and waiting. Give the students the assurance today that they will be able to go to school and not be let down. I ask, sir, that these students be encouraged rather than discouraged.

Mr. Speaker, Dr. Stuart Smith steps down at the end of August as Chairman of the Science Council. He has been an eloquent spokesman for science and fully understood the linkage between research and the market-place, the need to develop a knowledge intensive society, and he had an enormous capability for communicating to the general public the importance of science.
Last week he cited some of the accomplishments which he had encouraged and shaped: the creation of a Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology in the House of Commons; the creation of a basic framework for a national science and technology policy; the creation of a new Department of Industry, Science and Technology; establishment of a space agency as announced in the Speech from the Throne; and encouraging more science in the high schools and more young women in science.
Dr. Smith, the former Leader of the Liberal Party in Ontario, believes that science and technology have risen substantively on the list of government priorities, and he is reported as saying the present Conservative Government in the last 18 months has listened to him far more than the previous Liberal regime. I ask all those in this House to join me in thanking Dr. Smith for his enormous contribution to Canada and we wish him well in his new endeavours.

subtopic: POSITION OF EVANGELICAL FELLOWSHIP OF CANADA ON PROPOSED LEGISLATION
POSITION OF EVANGELICAL FELLOWSHIP OF CANADA ON PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week we heard from the Canadian Council of Churches, through its interchurch committee on refugees, the stand of the major Canadian denominations, Roman Catholic and Protestant, against Bill C-84 as it presently stands. We heard from them before on Bill C-55.
Now we hear from the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada. I have this telegram which says:
World Relief Canada, which serves as the refugee re-settlement arm of the Evangelical Fellowship of Canada, an association of 23 evangelical protestant denominations, strongly urges our Government not to pass Bills C-55 and C-84 as originally proposed. While we agree that abuses of our national largesse need to be prosecuted, we request that Parliament carefully consider amendments to the Bills which will strengthen fair treatment of bon fide refugees, and protect Canadians who helped them out of compassion and conscience.
R. E. Reimer World Relief Canada

PRESSURE TO REJECT TAX ON FOOD

subtopic: EXCLUSION OF HAY PRODUCERS-IRRIGATED LANDS ISSUE
EXCLUSION OF HAY PRODUCERS-IRRIGATED LANDS ISSUE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Special Canadian Grains Program helped to correct partially the intolerable situation created by the subsidy war between the EEC and the U.S. Farm Bill and will undoubtedly save hundreds of our farms, but it also hurt many farmers.
For example, many Canadian hay producers are on the verge of bankruptcy because the subsidies paid under the Grains Program enabled barley and green feed producers to sell at a reduced price to the feeders.
Second, the first payment failed to recognize the difference in yields of grains grown on stubble, on summer fallow, and on irrigated lands. This was partially corrected in the second payment when payment was made for the increased yields on irrigated lands providing the water was supplied by an irrigation district. The program refused to pay for the increased yields on lands that were irrigated by farmers who irrigated their lands through a co-op, an association, or privately, even though they grew the same crops and had similar yields and the same input costs. This is absolutely unfair and is infuriating hundreds of farmers.
Fairness is the essence of this Government's program and these unfair decisions should be corrected immediately.

Mr. Speaker, one of government's most vital functions is to maintain the integrity of our financial systems. Confidence in financial institutions underpins the operation of the capital markets and payment systems and confirms the credibility necessary to support the value of our currency. It is also important that Governments ensure that depositors are made clearly aware of the security of their deposits and the risks attached thereto.
With regard to the collapse of the Principal Group empire, many of the depositors have alleged that they were misled into believing that their deposits were 100 per cent safe and secure. We now know that such was not the case.
I urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to consider the proposal recently put forth by the Consumers' Association of Canada that, when depositors make an uninsured investment, they sign a waiver indicating that they are well aware that it is not covered by insurance.

August 24, 1987
While Governments cannot insulate consumers from shoddy or shady practices by financial institutions, they can reduce opportunities for such activities and minimize the financial damage caused by unscrupulous investment counsellors.

subtopic: CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO END RAIL STRIKE
CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO END RAIL STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the rail strike will cause incalculable damage to the nation, particularly to the economy of western Canada which relies so heavily on the bulk shipment of commodities such as grain, coal and potash.
Prairie farmers could ill afford the Thunder Bay and Vancouver closures and they certainly cannot afford this latest episode. Canada simply cannot afford to fritter away all the good economic progress achieved over the past three years- solid progress evidenced by the fact that 865,000 more Canadians are working today than three short years ago.
Strikes and lockouts are primitive, archaic weapons whereby the few can visit untold misery on the backs of all Canadians. Surely the time has come to find a better way to resolve labour-management disputes in essential services without these stoppages which hurt all Canadians.
1 urge the establishment of a parliamentary committee to study alternatives and make the appropriate recommendations. In the meantime, I urge legislation putting an early end to this sorry, unnecessary, and yet all too common situation.

subtopic: FUNDS NEEDED TO ESTABLISH TOXICOLOGY CENTRE
FUNDS NEEDED TO ESTABLISH TOXICOLOGY CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the long and sad saga of the Guelph-Toronto Toxicology centre goes on. The funds for this centre were cut from Environment Canada's budget in November, 1984, as you may recall. All of a sudden, in August, 1987, $12 million is found by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), not for a toxicology study centre but for a pest-control research facility in London, Ontario, to study biological and other pest-control programs aimed at reducing the reliance of farmers on pesticides in the long run.
This is good, but one wonders why the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) cannot find the funds necessary
for the development of the long overdue Guelph-Toronto toxicology centre. Toxic chemical contamination is becoming a fact of life, particularly in the Great Lakes Basin, which affects the population living around it. What we badly need is a centre to study the effects of toxic chemicals on human health.
Canadians are wondering why the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) cannot find funds to launch the Guelph-Toronto toxicology centre. Can it be attributed to ineptness?

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House today to draw to the attention of the Canadian public a situation which 1 feel is totally and unequivocally unacceptable. What I am referring to are the actions of some specific Members of this House who blatantly and repeatedly abuse their parliamentary privileges. They take advantage of the immunity granted to them by this House to viciously malign private citizens who have absolutely no means to defend themselves.
These character assassinations destroy the lives of not only the individuals but also their families and children. In many cases apologies are required after the fact, but this will never undo the damage.
I am referring directly to two recent incidents involving the defaming of two Petro-Canada employees and two members of CSIS, where I know this to be the case. On behalf of these people I would like to send a simple message to the fair-minded and honest citizens of our great country. When you hear degrading comments and slanderous remarks, do not take them at face value but consider the source.
Finally, I would like to apologize to the individuals who have fallen prey to the likes of those who use such cowardly and underhanded means. I refer to the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) and the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps).
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Hon. Members will know that while there is a lot of latitude used in Statements by Members and, in general, something that is a complaint can, of course, be mentioned, but it is not appropriate to identify a particular Member.
August 24, 1987

Mr. Speaker, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans has been on the chopping block since the 1984 election. No other Department has lost so much of its budget. The slashing of staff, budgets and research is leading to chaos in our commercial, sport and food fisheries.
There is an urgent need for watershed management boards involving all user groups, especially on the Skeena River. The pressure on some wild stocks of salmon and steelhead has reached the breaking point. Many runs, in fact entire races of these anadromous species are becoming extinct.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) does not blink at giving the Reichman brothers a $1 billion tax holiday with the "little Egypt bump" on Gulf Oil, $1 billion to bail out the Northland and Canadian Commercial Banks and a SI billion tax holiday to the big banks for their mismanagement of loans outside Canada. What about our fisheries? How about a break for those who derive their livelihood, their sports activity and food from the seas and rivers?
Time and again the Minister has been asked to establish a process to bring all fishing sectors together in the spirit of avoiding resource conflicts and possible confrontation. No initiative has been shown. While the Minister holidays and negotiates lower flows on our rivers, steelhead and salmon runs disappear. Once again what western Canadians prize in our fisheries this Conservative Government neglects and destroys. How about a "blink" for our fish?

Mr. Speaker, most of the opposition to Bill C-22, the patent drug legislation, has been based on the falsehood that consumers will be adversely affected. The Liberals and New Democrats have been practising political opportunism of the most despicable kind. They are preying on the fears of seniors and the ill. However, it is important to note that there is a lot of support for the Bill as passed by the House of Commons in May.
This morning, in Charlottetown, the General Council of the Canadian Medical Association, which represents 43,000 Canadian doctors, passed the following resolution unanimously:
That the Canadian Medical Association declares its support in principle for Bill C-22 as a measure which in the long term is likely to benefit the health of Canadians.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, those who work in the health care field, and can offer an objective opinion, support Bill C-
22.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians woke up this morning to the very unwelcome news that the national railways were shut down due to striking unions.
This is bad news for the people of northern Ontario, as it is for others across the country. The resource based industries of the North depend greatly on the rail service. In the riding of Timiskaming the iron ore mine of Adams-Sherman, which has 800 workers, ships pellets to Hamilton. Lumber mills across the North and the Ontario Northland Railway, which is a regional railroad, are also heavily dependent on rail service.
I trust that the Government will act to ensure a speedy resolution of this labour dispute. We would like to see all Canadians back on track.

subtopic: COMMEMORATE STAMP-REFUSAL OF ANGLICAN CHURCH'S APPLICATION
COMMEMORATE STAMP-REFUSAL OF ANGLICAN CHURCH'S APPLICATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a short statement to make with regard to the Post Office and to its commemorative stamps program.
Most Canadians would have been shocked, as I was, to read that the Anglican Church was denied a commemorative stamp, an historic stamp. I cannot for the life of me figure out why. Other major churches and institutions have been accorded such stamps. The Post Office has given these stamps for many different purposes, so why could it not add one more stamp to the historic stamps it will issue this year? Why is it at least appearing to discriminate against the Anglican Church? I find this difficult to understand.
I hope that the Government will take the Post Office president by the collar, shake him up a bit and say: "Pay a little attention to the people of Canada and stop being deaf when people bring their concerns to you and ask you for a small action that could reflect the historic events of our country".

August 24, 1987
Oral Questions

What does the Government intend to do to try to get an early negotiated settlement of this strike? For example, does the Government intend to modify or to extend the mandate of the mediator? What else does the Government plan to do to settle this matter?

subsubtopic: RAIL STRIKE-POSSIBILITY OF SETTLEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subsubtopic: RAIL STRIKE-POSSIBILITY OF SETTLEMENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL'S CORPORATE PLAN-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF WORKFORCE
CANADIAN NATIONAL'S CORPORATE PLAN-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF WORKFORCE
speechtext:
My question is directed to the Minister of Transport. In looking at CN's corporate plan we see a massive reduction of 25 per cent of its workforce over the next five years.
August 24, 1987

How can the Minister expect the union leaders to agree to sign a collective agreement that does not give the workers job security?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL'S CORPORATE PLAN-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF WORKFORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is the obligation of the management of Canadian National, as it is of the management of CP, to manage the company in the best manner they can, given all the circumstances that they have to face.
It is well known in the railway industry that there has been a reduction in the number of people who work in the railway industries in Canada, the United States, and other countries as the nature of the transportation system has changed. Trucking has become more competitive, shipping has become more competitive, therefore management has had to deal with that regrettable situation.
CN has indicated that in the future it will have to be very careful with respect to how many people it employs, and attempt to increase productivity. All of this helps the shippers of Canada, helps to make Canada competitive, and helps to make Canadian products competitive. It helps to sell grain abroad at a competitive price. The hon. gentleman knows this.
As to security under the contract, there were provisions in the contract that are still in effect that deal with that question. It is now a matter for negotiation between the parties, and I don't think I should say anything further.

subtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH PROGRAM TO ASSIST EARLY RETIREES
OPPORTUNITY TO ESTABLISH PROGRAM TO ASSIST EARLY RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister has just taken the Pontius Pilate way out, and I think it is unacceptable that he should shift the entire responsibility for the loss of 12,000 jobs on to CN.
Would the Minister be prepared to provide immediately an early retirement program for railway employees who will be directly affected by the massive deregulation imposed by the Conservative Government? Could the Minister accept his responsibility and do something for the railway employees?

dispute. That is the system of law that was left to us by the previous Government, and with which we agree.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. I am sure most Canadians want an answer to that question.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):

August 24, 1987
Oral Questions TRADE

subtopic: IMPOSITION OF UNITED STATES TARIFF ON CANADIAN POTASH IMPORTS
IMPOSITION OF UNITED STATES TARIFF ON CANADIAN POTASH IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister for International Trade I will direct my question to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is fully aware that on Friday the United States announced the imposition of up to a devastating 85 per cent tariff on potash exports to that country, which will have an effect upon $350 million worth of exports and affect up to 4,000 jobs in New Brunswick, Saskatchewan and other provinces.
The Minister for International Trade said the reaction of the Canadian Government was only one of disappointment. Does that mean the Canadian Government is in effect agreeing with the United States' determination of this matter, or does it intend to fight through every possible avenue and recourse, and not cave in like it did in the softwood lumber case in which it imposed a tax on ourselves and set a precedent that has resulted in this kind of further action being imposed on Canadian producers?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: IMPOSITION OF UNITED STATES TARIFF ON CANADIAN POTASH IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly the Government is very disappointed and is reviewing the case very carefully. I think the Hon. Member is aware that this is one step in a very complicated quasi-judicial process, but I think it is fair to point out that all this leads to the fact that we do need a comprehensive trading arrangement.
This decision is a product of the current trading relationship we have with the United States and we are trying to confront this issue in the broadest possible sense by working out a solution which would be encompassed in a framework that would provide a comprehensive trading relationship between our two countries with an adequate dispute resolving mechanism. The Hon. Member should be supporting that initiative rather than picking holes in it.

subtopic: IMPOSITION OF UNITED STATES TARIFF ON CANADIAN POTASH IMPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I only want to point out to the Deputy Prime Minister that it appears that the more we negotiate, the more we get hit by American trade actions which are having an incredibly damaging effect on all parts of the Canadian economy. So much for the negotiations when all we do is pay the price and they get the benefits.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister if the Government intends to provide any form of contingency protection for the potash producers in order to ensure that they stay in business and continue their operations, or is in fact any support that might be provided prohibited under the proposed free trade negotiations in which the Government is presently engaged?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister for International Trade has pointed out, she and officials will be working very closely with the Government of Saskatchewan, the potash companies and all those involved to try to work together toward presenting the best possible case.
There is simply no question about the fact that there is a strong protectionist sentiment in the United States, and I know my hon. friend across the way shares some of those political views with his colleagues south of the border. What we in this country need more than anything, and it is becoming clearer every day, is a comprehensive trade arrangement with a dispute resolving mechanism that can see these kinds of issues resolved once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, what the people of Canada need is a Government that will just for once stand up for their interests in trade with the United States. Apropos of that, I would like to ask the Minister a specific question. Since this is damaging to an industry that exports about $500 million worth of products each year and affects the people of New Brunswick as well as the people of Saskatchewan, what is the Government of Canada planning to do concretely on a bilateral basis with the United States to get it to reverse this totally unjustified whack at another Canadian export industry that happens to be doing very well in fair competition?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it should be pointed out that this was not an initiative taken by the U.S. Government, it was an initiative taken by the industry. It is the first step in a long series of steps through a very complicated quasi- judicial process. As I indicated to the previous questioner, the Government of Canada stands very solidly in support of the Canadian industry, the Government of Saskatchewan and individuals in trying to put the best case forward on behalf of Canada and the potash producers of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as the Deputy Prime Minister knows very well, this follows a long series of unfortunate and unfair decisions on shakes and shingles, tubular steel, softwood, pork and a whole range of products. The last time a major decision was made against us was on the softwood issue. The Government then said it would protest the American decision at GATT. Instead of doing that, it caved in and, in a masochistic way, imposed a self-inflicted punishment on Canadians in order to mesh with the American decision.
Since the Government promised it would take the earlier unfair decision to GATT and it did not, will we get a concrete promise now about what the Canadian Government will do to
August 24, 1987

protect potash producers? Will the Government deliver on that promise?
