speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather interesting that the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party would have rather seen the $600 million flow to the United States than stay in Canada. That is certainly contrary to the views of this Government and the views of most Canadian Premiers.
While the Hon. Member seems to take great satisfaction in bearing bad news, may 1 just point out that the Canada West Foundation which has just done a study on the trade negotiations has indicated that in the Province of Saskatchewan, about which the Hon. Leader of the NDP seems to be concerned, a comprehensive trade arrangement with the United States would produce about 55,000 new jobs. It also points out that failure to secure an agreement would cost the Canadian economy some 350,000 jobs. Why does the Hon. Leader of the NDP, not get on with it and support the protection of Canadian jobs and the Government's initiatives?
1 think the workers of Canada would laud him for his efforts.

Mr. Speaker, this Party favours an approach that has worked quite well, and that is to deal with the United States on a multilateral, multinational basis in order to get fair trade all around the world and not just a special deal with the United States that is bound to work to our disadvantage.
Since the Deputy Prime Minister has expressed concern for the impact on the workers of Saskatchewan and New Brunswick who will potentially be affected by this, and I have no doubt that he is quite genuine about it, what plans is the Government considering putting in place if worse comes to worst and there are significant lay-offs in this sector of those two provinces as a result of this unfair American decision?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Leader is a lecturer in a classroom yet he does not understand a few lessons from an ordinary layman like myself. I have tried to point out that the Canada West Foundation has indicated that a free trade arrangement would save some 350,000 jobs in Canada and produce some 55,000 new jobs-
I will give you federal studies that show the opposite.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Chamber of Commerce, the Economic Council of Canada and other organizations like that share the same view. I am not trying to argue that black is white, but obviously the Leader of the NDP is.
I would like to point out that in connection with the reference to GATT, the Minister has indicated in a press release that we will be reviewing the Commerce decision,
Oral Questions
particularly with a view to ensuring that it is consistent with the United States' obligations under GATT. 1 think that should respond to the earlier question raised by the Hon. Member.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-POSTPONEMENT OF MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL PREMIERS

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-POSTPONEMENT OF MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL PREMIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. Speaking of studies, the Government's own study from its Department of Regional Industrial Expansion shows that a lot more industries and a lot more jobs would be hurt than would be helped by the Government's free trade initiative.
If the Prime Minister is so convinced that the provincial Premiers support what he is doing, why has he unilaterally and without consulting with the provincial Premiers postponed a meeting with them to consider a draft text of a free trade agreement from an agreed on date of September 8 to September 14? If the Prime Minister has made such a postponement, could it be that deep in his own heart he realizes that giving the Premiers enough time to study any draft text of a free trade agreement would show that it is not a good deal for Canada and should not be proceeded with?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-POSTPONEMENT OF MEETING WITH PROVINCIAL PREMIERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose my hon. friend would want to square the comments he has made with those made recently by Premier Bourassa, the Liberal Premier of Quebec, who said that the absence of a free trade arrangement would mean the irreversible decline of Quebec in Canada economically. When the free trade initiative is supported by the Premiers as it is, I think my hon. friend would do well to listen to their voices and to the objective studies.
My hon. friend referred to the Economic Council of Canada which predicted a net increase of some 350,000 new jobs in Canada and a decline in unemployment, particularly in our far-flung regions. This is why we are seeking so actively a free trade initiative. It means jobs and prosperity for Canadians, particularly in those areas that have not had the kinds of low unemployment rates we have been able to bring to southern Ontario, for example. I know my hon. friend would want fairness to prevail in employment.
Regarding the time, we are seeking an occasion on which the First Ministers can review carefully, in all the time required, any trade arrangement, if indeed we conclude one. We are looking for a mutually acceptable date.

subtopic: STUDY BY PREMIERS OF DRAFT AGREEMENT

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF REPORTED CORRESPONDENCE ON CANADIAN POLICY WITH RESPECT TO AUTO TRADE
REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF REPORTED CORRESPONDENCE ON CANADIAN POLICY WITH RESPECT TO AUTO TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. 1 have here copies of correspondence between the Office of the U.S. Representative for External Trade and Congressman John Dingwall. This correspondence, although it is a year old, is proof of a concerted attack on key elements of Canada's policy on the automobile industry as reflected in the Auto Pact.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OF REPORTED CORRESPONDENCE ON CANADIAN POLICY WITH RESPECT TO AUTO TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure, is the Hon. Member referring to a report, which is about a year old, raised by the CBC? If so, that is a bit of an old news item and there is really nothing new to add. This matter was debated to some extent a year ago and nothing has changed.
The position of the Canadian Government is the same. We have not raised the Auto Pact. Neither has the U.S., I am advised. If issues surrounding the Auto Pact are raised which would improve Canada's position, of course we would be prepared to sit down and talk about it.

Mr. Speaker, let me make clear that the reference was to the calling into question of the Canadian duty remission scheme. Will the Canadian Government, during the free trade negotiations, accept the American position that in order to have such a pact the duty remission scheme must be cancelled? That scheme was intended to produce and has produced Canadian jobs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The Hon. Member's Party was invited to sit in on a confidential briefing requested by the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville. His Party refused. I think it is really inappropriate to try to hammer out a very complex arrangement on the floor of the House of Commons.

August 24, 1987

Government to withdraw its proposed sales tax on food. Over the weekend the Quebec Conservative caucus finally saw the light and came out against this food tax.

speechtext: Poor Marcel, he has put his foot in it again-

Considering that the Quebec Progressive Conservative caucus has endorsed the position of my caucus and has stated its opposition to a sales tax on food, is the Prime Minister
Oral Questions
aware of the fact that 93 per cent of all Canadians are opposed to a food tax and can he assure them that the government will not introduce a sales tax on food?
The Hon. Member is somewhat late in asking such a question.

speakeroldname: The Right Hon. Brian Mulroney (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis is asking me to point out to the Hon. Member that he is late. It is done.
The Minister has already answered the question. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Prime Minister. So far, recognized groups have proposed amendments to the Meech Lake Accord but all have been rejected by the Government. Today, the

August 24, 1987
Oral Questions
Supreme Court of Canada has revealed its opinion-the same as that of the Official Opposition-that the Meech Lake Accord should be amended to allow the Territories to submit lists of candidates, including judges and lawyers, for the Supreme Court of Canada. Does the Prime Minister also reject the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEECH LAKE ACCORD-SUPREME COURT'S OPINION-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should put his question in the proper context. I do not agree with the premise of the question. Not having seen the total report and having read only the press reports on the report of the Canadian Bar Association, I would not draw the same conclusions.
The reality is that the recommendation of the Canadian Bar Association had to do with eligibility of members of the Bars of the Northwest Territory and Yukon. Our position has been clear. We consider them eligible for appointment. That, purely and simply, is the situation which faces us with this report. If the Supreme Court judges agree with us, I am very grateful.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the Minister will look into precisely what has been recommended. As 1 understand it, it has indeed been expressed as the opinion of the Supreme Court of Canada that the territories should be able to submit lists directly.
Is the Government prepared to accept that very sensible suggestion so that, like the provinces, the territories can suggest names to be considered by the federal Government for appointment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members will know, this is the subject of litigation at the present time. The position of the territories is before the courts, initiated by them. I think it is highly improper for us to be commenting on issues before the courts.
I have indicated our position which has been set forth by counsel on behalf of the federal Government which sustains the position I have articulated. I think we should now leave the matter to the courts to resolve the exact legal position.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and is with regard to the 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber bound for the U.S. This is the largest self-imposed fiscal penalty in world trade history
and costs our largest industry and largest source of balance of trade $600 million a year in penalty.
Is the Prime Minister suggesting to Canadians that, following the signing of a free trade agreement with the United States, he will lift this self-imposed penalty against our softwood lumber?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend refers to a self-inflicted penalty. Under one proposal this $600 million a year was going to go into the coffers of the United States. Under the proposal worked out by the Government in co-operation with the provinces the $600 million remains in Canada very much under provincial control and, in large measure, to improve the situation of our forests and our competitiveness. Surely as a British Columbian my hon. friend knows that and would agree with the thrust of that action.
In larger terms, objective studies indicate that a free trade arrangement with the United States of America, while not perfect, would bring 300,000 or 400,000 new jobs to Canada. 1 think that is highly desirable. In addition to that, if we are successful, it would normalize a situation and would allow the resolution of disputes such as the one my hon. friend has mentioned which, in the normal course of a better trading arrangement, would not arise.
We are pursuing this with such vigour, first, because we believe that the prosperity of Canada and the creation of jobs for young Canadians depend very much upon this kind of initiative. Second, it would eliminate the kind of capricious action taken in the past. However, I think a wise Government has managed to keep the proceeds of that here for reinvestment in Canadian forests.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Prime Minister. It is a very simple question. Up until January 1 of this year we always had unrestricted free trade in softwood lumber with the United States. If the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States reach and sign a free trade agreement, will the Prime Minister then lift this 15 per cent self-imposed tariff off Canadian softwood lumber bound for the United States?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend can correct me if I am mistaken. He seems to speak disapprovingly of what was done with regard to the softwood lumber issue. My understanding is that that was very much endorsed by the IWA in British Columbia and the provincial members of the New Democratic Party in his province. It was endorsed as well by all of the Premiers and the Government of Canada. It clearly met national objectives which were, at that time, to resolve a very strong irritant and to keep the money here in Canada for reinvestment in our forest area.
August 24, 1987

Can the matter be resolved in the future? Obviously the object of concluding a comprehensive trade arrangement with the United States is to eliminate irritants and the kinds of capricious actions which we have seen in the past which continue to debilitate our relationship and preclude the possibility of further trade arrangements. If we are successful, as a necessary follow-up we would want to try to deal with each one of these irritants to make the situation even better than it can be under a trade arrangement.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the speech delivered on Friday by the Minister of corporate affairs-and perhaps he should be renamed Minister of multinational affairs-is one which deserves-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has the floor.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, the speech given in this House on Friday morning by the Minister of corporate affairs is one that deserves attention, study and definitely a rebuttal. I was stunned to hear the Minister imply in his speech that this piece of legislation, once approved, would protect Canadians from price increases in drugs and medicines. As can be seen in Hansard of August 21, page 8282, the Minister stated with respect to Bill C-22:
Under our scheme the Drug Prices Review Board will be examining those drugs and keeping the price increases of them at less than the cost of living.
August 24, 1987

That is quite a statement. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, a Minister of the Crown committing this piece of legislation to the extent of protecting Canadians from drug price increases. I looked at the Bill to find the basis for such a statement but nowhere could I find a clause in Bill C-22 that would corroborate that particular statement by the Minister.
Proposed Section 41.18, with respect to the Patent Medicine Prices Review Board, contains a lengthy description of what this Bill will do. It is over two pages long and includes a description of the powers of the board, specifically proposed Section 41.23(4), but nowhere in the Bill is there a scintilla of an indication to justify the Minister's statement that drug prices would not increase more than the cost of living. In fact, nowhere in the clause with respect to the powers of the board is there an indication that this particular board would have powers to control prices. Proposed Section 41.23(4) in the Bill states:
The Board has, with respect to the attendance, swearing and examination of witnesses, the production and inspection of documents, the enforcement of its orders and other matters necessary or proper for the due exercise of its jurisdiction, all such powers, rights and privileges as are vested in a superior court of record.
That is all. Nowhere in this clause are powers given to the board to control prices, let alone the power to roll back prices.
1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, in light of this, how can the Minister of the Crown make the promise to Canadians that price increases will not be greater than the increase in the cost of living? Nowhere in this Bill are these powers given to the board. The only power given to this board, according to the proposed legislation, is to review. You know as well as 1 do, Mr. Speaker, that the power to "review" prices is just what the word means. It means to review prices. As indicated in the Bill, it is necessary to report probably once a year to Parliament and to the Minister the result of one's reviews. But this board has not been given the power, anywhere in the Bill, to control or to roll back prices once the legislation comes into effect.
It is no wonder why, when enumerating the individuals and organizations who are in support of this legislation, the Minister could not include such important organizations as the Consumers' Association of Canada. He could not include in his list of supporters, who were, by the way, mainly individuals and organizations interested in international trade, the Canadian Hospital Association. Nor could he include the Canadian Anti-Poverty Association or the Canadian Council on Social Development. He could not include the National Pensioners & Senior Citizens Federation on his list. I ask Hon. Members why he could not include these organizations. Why could he not include the Canadian Drug Manufacturers Association which has written to you, Mr. Speaker, and to every Member of Parliament since last October? Why could he not include that organization? It was for a very clear reason. These are basic, fundamental organizations which are not in favour of Bill C-22, for understandable reasons.
Patent Act
I submit that one of the basic reasons is that there is no power given to this board to control the prices once this law comes into effect. All that it can do, and this is where the Minister did not indicate to the House the facts as they are, is review the prices, as its name implies, and nothing more. It is a very poor thing for a Minister of the Crown to create an impression by making a statement in the House of Commons that is so far removed from the facts.
I suppose that is one of the reasons why on Friday the Minister could not include among those who support this measure your own provincial Government, Mr. Speaker, which is not in support of this Bill. That Government certainly cannot be considered to be composed of a bunch of rabid socialists, as you well know, Mr. Speaker. He could not include the Government of Manitoba. Nor could he include the Government of Ontario. He could not include the Government of Prince Edward Island. Not only that, he could not include two other Tory governments; he could not include the Tory Government of Prince Edward Island, as I mentioned, or the Tory Governments of Newfoundland and New Brunswick. That makes six provincial Governments which are against the legislation we are now discussing.
That should send a message to the Minister. It should indicate that these provincial governments are preoccupied with the impact of this particular legislation on the consumer, the average person, and, of course, on the prices of pharmaceuticals. If it has an impact on prices then it means that those provincial Governments have come to the conclusion that proposed Section 41.23(4) gives the board no power. It gives it the power just to call witnesses and to take a matter under investigation. But this board does not have substantial, fundamental and important powers for the protection of the public, namely, controlling prices and, where necessary, rolling them back. Therefore, support for this Bill may be an indication to Members of the House of how weak it is, particularly since six out of ten provincial governments are not in support of it.
An interesting letter was sent to us last December from Vancouver by the Building and Construction Trades Council in which the Secretary-Treasurer of the Council included a copy of his letter to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) in which he states:
On behalf of our members and other wage earners in our communities we are extremely disturbed by the proposed amendments to drug patent legislation.
He goes on to state:
There can be no doubt that the effect of these changes will be to increase drug prices to the consumer. Since most working people have received little or nothing in the way of wage increases in the last few years and since hundreds of thousands of working people continue to try to exist on Unemployment Insurance payments, increases in the price of drugs, which would represent cuts to the present incomes of all Canadians-drugs, an absolute essential for many of our people-would represent a cruel and unjustified hardship.
One can well understand the reason why a letter such as this has been sent. It is why I took the first opportunity this

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
morning of asking the Parliamentary Secretary to indicate to us where in the Bill there is the power to control prices. She was not able to answer that question because she cannot find that assurance in the Bill; It is not there. That matter has to be put on record and has to be brought to the attention of the public in a clear manner now that we are again debating it.
I would now like to deal with another passage of the Minister's speech which he gave the other day. He said that the Senate is threatening to veto this Bill. On the one hand he says that the Senate is threatening to veto the Bill while on the other he says that he has a number of amendments he would like to negotiate with the Senate. One cannot negotiate amendments with the Senate, as the Minister proposed on Friday, and then at the same time the Senate is threatening to veto the Bill. That is not what the Senate is doing.
The fact of the matter is that here we have the Senate exercising its constitutional rights and duties, as it has done with other Bills: It has done quite well in that respect. In other Bills when it has come forward with a number of amendments, the Government has accepted them. Consistent with that role in the past, which is constitutional and which is within the right and the responsibility of the Upper House, the Senate has come forward with a number of amendments resulting from a number of public consultations. In doing so now it has put to the House of Commons these amendments which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has the nerve to describe on the one hand as a veto, while accepting certain of them on the other hand. The Minister of corporate affairs cannot have it both ways. He cannot call this action by the Senate a veto, and at the same time consider accepting certain amendments in to the Senate package.
The Senate has proposed a number of measures which indicate its perception of the public feeling today concerning the matter of drugs. In essence, it put forward a number of recommendations that were contained in the Eastman report which would protect the public in a manner that is better than Bill C-22. It would allow the Canadian manufacturers of generic drugs to produce drugs in a shorter period of time after they have been developed by a single company, namely, after four years instead of after ten years as was proposed in the Bill. This will permit greater competition, and the lowering of drug prices.
This is the essence of the Senate proposal, as far as the consumer is concerned. The Senate is also preoccupied with jobs. It seems to me that the Senate has made an eminently reasonable proposal for the development and the creation of jobs. As the Minister of corporate affairs has claimed, it is not a measure that will deny jobs to Canadians. On the contrary, the set of proposals that emanated from the Senate would permit the creation of jobs in Canada.
The Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) in his speech on Friday made reference to the 48
amendments that he put forward in committee on behalf of the Official Opposition. Having fought for the amendments, and having lost them, it is quite understandable that those 48 amendments could not be lost and forgotten. Evidently, the Senators became aware of this enormous exercise and effort on the part of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. The Senators have picked up some of the cause. Through the Upper Chamber, they did what was not possible to achieve in the Tory dominated committee which studied Bill C-22. In that respect, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton- East Richmond did a phenomenal amount of work in pioneering the 48 amendments.
When a piece of legislation triggers a large number of amendments, it means that it is a poor piece of legislation. It is not only a partisan, momentary aberration to oppose, these amendments were well thought out. They were announced at second reading in the House by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. They were carried out in committee, but only to the point of proposing them because they were voted down. The Senate action has to be seen within this broader context.
We would like to see a piece of legislation that does not favour only the interests of the multinationals. That is the fundamental point that must be kept in mind. We have fought, as has the Senate, for legislation that looks beyond the interest of the multinational corporations. We would like to see a piece of legislation that looks at the pharmaceutical industry, at manufacturing in Canada, with an opportunity that goes to other active elements in the pharmaceutical sector which are not multinational corporations. There are many of them, and they have to be taken into account. It is important that we at least attempt to pursue and defend the interests of the nonmultinationals. They are employers of some considerable extent. They represent a number of Canadians who have to see a future opportunity by way of legislation that also guarantees and continues their reason for existence.
In essence, Bill C-22 is an ill-conceived measure. It has been debated back and forth for several months. I can understand the frustration of the Minister of corporate affairs in seeing his measures not accepted. But the message for him is that perhaps his legislation is not acceptable. It is not in the interest of the public, and it needs to be changed.
I am sure if the Minister were reasonable, flexible, and looked at the proposals one by one from the Senate, and considered those that are in the interest of the consumer, and the people who ultimate have to buy these drugs, he would see the merits of preserving the character of the Canadian system.
Comparing our system with the system that prevails south of the border, which was so well described by Ralph Nader when he appeared on television the other day, Mr. Nader stated the merits of preserving the character of the Canadian retail and price structure system, and not adopting the system that prevails south of the border. Mr. Nader criticized the system in the United States when he said that they would rather have
August 24, 1987

the Canadian system for pharmaceuticals and protection of the consumer, and not see Canada follow the system that presently dominates in the United States.
For all these reasons, we are very critical of the position taken on Friday by the Minister of corporate affairs. The Minister is giving the public the wrong impression as to the powers of the prices review board. It cannot be found in the existing legislation. The Minister is criticizing the Senate for having done something that is perfectly constitutional. Not only is it constitutional but, as a Chamber of sober second thought, it is its duty. The Minister is also critical of the Senate for having provided the House with a set of amendments which ultimately would protect the interest of the average Canadian consumer.

speechtext: On debate, the Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. White).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to take part in the debate this afternoon, but at the same time 1 am sorry that it had to take place in the first instance.
As it was passed by the House on May 6, Bill C-22 took a balanced view of the pharmaceutical industry. It provides for increased research and development, and chemical manufacturing, and continued growth of the generic companies. Bill C-22 is also committed to increasing consumer protection, and protecting provincial health care budgets.
Under the recent amendments proposed by the Senate, the current situation would change very little, if at all. The status quo would be maintained, which was confirmed by a memo sent to the Fiberal caucus from the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall). More importantly, Canadians would be deprived of the eventual benefits that would result if the original Bill C-22 was passed by the House. Indeed, the protection of individual and provincial health plans included in Bill C-22 has been completely ignored in the Senate proposals.
There have been many concerns raised over the impact of Bill C-22 on the prices of drugs. Specifically, someone stated that this policy will remove generic competition from the pharmaceutical market-place. Several months ago, a Minister of the Crown from the Province of Manitoba wrote a letter to the editor of my local paper in Swan River which stated that Bill C-22 would prohibit generic drugs in Canada. Such a statement from a provincial Minister of the Crown in Manitoba is clearly and completely false and untrue. Any such claims are simply not true. According to the legislation, all generic drugs on the market prior to June 27, 1986, will continue to be available. Any comments to the contrary are simply not true. In addition to those drugs, about 40 more could be subject to generic competition over the next five years. I emphasize that these drugs could be available because the profit motive comes into effect. If one suffers from a condition that requires a particular drug which is not a best seller, then a generic copy
Patent Act
will not be available because the only motive that drives a generic company is the profit motive. If the drug is not rich enough it will not attract a generic competitor.
One must also remember that there is nothing in this policy that would cause the price of drugs now on the market to increase. Quite frankly, consumers will not suffer because of this legislation.
This will be especially true in the area of improved health care. It is very important to note that as current as this morning, the General Council of the Canadian Medical Association, meeting in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, passed the following brief unanimous resolution which states: "That the Canadian Medical Association declares its support in principle for Bill C-22 as a measure which, in the long term, is likely to benefit the health of Canadians".
Under Bill C-22 as passed by this House, new drugs and new therapies will be introduced earlier. The need for hospitalization will be reduced and perhaps even the need for surgery will be reduced because we will have new drugs to cure old problems. An example of this is the drug Cimetidine. It was first marketed under the name Tagamet by Smith, Kline and French. It has been estimated that the introduction of Tagamet has saved Up to $130 million in surgery. It is very important to consider that there will be many other drugs that will contribute to the health care of Canadians.
It is also important to note that Smith, Kline and French has been brutalized by the present system of compulsory licensing. It has had to close plants and has lost millions of dollars in sales and has lost Canadian workers.
This decreased need for hospitalization because of new and better medication will be even more important over the next several decades as baby boomers become seniors and place substantially heavier demands on our health care system. It has been estimated that by the year 2000 the average drug store will depend on senior citizens for 75 per cent of its business. This must be kept in mind as we discuss Bill C-22 and its benefits for the health care system.
The discovery of cures and treatments for diseases afflicting Canadians, especially our seniors, is essential to our well-being. With the increased research and development under Bill C-22, Canada will play a larger role in the field of medical discovery.
Canadian consumers enjoy fair drug prices mainly because of the purchasing power of the provinces, which buy 60 per cent of all the drugs in Canada and provide coverage for almost all our country's senior citizens. I should also note that this downward pressure on prices will continue in the marketplace under Bill C-22.
Without some improvement in our country's health care system, provincial Governments will be faced with an even heavier burden for hospital care. Amendments such as those proposed by the Senate recently would impede improvements

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
to the well-being of Canadians and, in turn, lead to higher costs for taxpayers.
Bill C-22, as it was passed by this House on May 6, takes into consideration all of these aspects. First, it provides the incentive for research and development which will enable Canada to benefit from new world class technologies in the fields of bio-tech, medicine, and health care.
Second, it strengthens consumer protection by ensuring that all patent drug prices are reviewed, not only those for which there is generic competition. If one goes to a drug store in Canada and randomly picks 100 drugs off the shelf, 93 of them would have no generic competitor for the reason I stated a few minutes ago. The only motive that drives the generic company is profit and, at present, only 7 per cent by volume and 20 per cent by dollar value are rich enough to attract generics.
The drug prices review board will be established to monitor the price of all patented drugs, not just that 7 per cent that are best sellers and rich enough to attract generics.
Under the current policy, consumers have no way of knowing whether they are paying a fair price for that 93 per cent of drugs that have no generic copy. Without the establishment of the drug prices review board, prices would be higher than they might otherwise be.
Doctor Eastman, who prepared the report some three or four years ago, will be the head of that board. During his testimony to the legislative committee that was considering Bill C-22, Doctor Eastman also said that he was confident that the drug prices review board would be beneficial to Canadian consumers.
The provinces will also benefit from the original Bill C-22. For instance, Bill C-22 proposed transitional payments of $25 million a year for the first four years of the policy, leading up to its first full review by Cabinet. This is additional security against any adjustment that may be made to provincial drug plans and ultimately additional security for those individual consumers who are covered by provincial plans.
The legislation that was sent to the Senate recognizes the importance of the provincial role in health care and the provision of drugs at reasonable prices to all Canadians.
The Bill allows for the establishment of an advisory panel which will be made up of persons from a variety of backgrounds. This panel would make recommendations on appointments to the prices review board. Furthermore, the board is required to notify the provincial Ministers of Health of any hearing the board will hold.
The provinces also have the statutory right to present evidence to the board. As the largest purchasers of medicine, they are, therefore, guaranteed a voice in the proceedings.
As well as protecting the provinces and consumers against unduly high drug prices, Bill C-22 will direct research and development expenditures to every region of Canada. For
instance, as a result of the new policy, the innovative sector has recently announced commitments of almost $800 million to be spent on research in hospitals, universities and research centres across Canada over the next ten years. The $800 million is not an investment in just one facility. There will be more than $200 million in Quebec, upwards of $80 million in British Columbia, at least $70 million in the Maritimes, about $100 million in Alberta, $250 million in Ontario, and approximately $50 million in my home province of Manitoba. Chemical manufacturing, which will also be stimulated by these provisions, will add to these figures.
The New Democratic Government of Manitoba has been vehemently opposed to Bill C-22. In my opinion, it has been opposed for purely political reasons and it is nothing but a political opportunist. In fact, one of the Ministers of the Crown in Manitoba recently told a group of researchers at the St. Boniface Hospital in Winnipeg that Bill C-22 is doing the right thing, but the NDP could not resist the political opportunity that presented itself in this situation. In my opinion, that is despicable.
Bill C-22 would provide a policy that does not rely on government grants or government subsidies and takeovers. It is the private sector at its best, doing what it does best. This new policy is another step in the Government's efforts to promote sustained economic growth and job-creation while providing for the protection of Canadian consumers.
On the other hand, the Senate proposal uses the status quo of generic copying as the only way of lowering drug prices. Unfortunately, this system does not adequately protect all individuals. It is important to reiterate that generic companies only copy those drugs with a high sales volume and they do no research. Another witness who appeared before the committee, Doctor Chretien, a clinical researcher from Quebec, said that generic companies do zero research. The few dollars they report as going into research are going into nothing other than quality control.
In fact, with the Senate amendments, companies will be able to charge whatever introductory price they wish for new drugs because generic companies take at least four to five years to copy a product. They wait that long until a market and profit has been established for a particular drug. In addition, some drugs never face competition because they are the so-called orphan drugs that are not big sellers and do not attract generic competition. Therefore, consumers of these products do not benefit from the compulsory licensing system as it exists today.
The Senate has also recommended that the royalty rate paid by generic firms be increased to about 14 per cent from the current 4 per cent. This measure could lead to an immediate 10 per cent increase in the price of generic drugs and a corresponding increase in prices of equivalent brand name products.
As well, the royalty scheme proposed will generate only a very small amount of money for new research and development. In fact, the Eastman Commission of Inquiry estimated
August 24, 1987

that if the royalty fund had been fully mature in 1983, about $6 million would have been available for distribution for new research and development projects. That $6 million is only one-fifth of the total increase in costs. It is an insignificant portion of the $1.4 billion increase in research and development that could result from Bill C-22.
The Senate proposal focuses almost entirely on drug costs. While this is very important and is recognized in the original Bill C-22 by the extension of consumer protection, there was no consideration by the Senate committee of the impact of new medicines on reducing hospital costs. 1 mentioned this earlier and referred specifically to Tagamet and its $130-million-per-year savings in now unnecessary stomach surgery.
The 1985 report of the Eastman Commission stated that the royalty proposal would have cost over $30 million in 1983 alone. Those costs would have been borne directly by consumers and provinces. This is clear evidence that the Senate proposal is not cost-free as some people would have us believe. To summarize that, in fact, for every $1 generated by the Senate's royalty fund, consumers would be paying an extra $6.20. That increased cost to consumers would amount to over $1 billion in the next 10 years.
In conclusion, I would like to say that I am very disappointed that the Senate, after such a considerable delay that threatens the viability of already-announced investment plans, continues to take a position on Bill C-22 which gives such little regard to the facts. As you know, Mr. Speaker, there has been substantial discussion of the cost estimates of Bill C-22 among the many interested parties. The Canadian Drug Manufacturers' Association and members of the Opposition in the House of Commons have quoted exaggerated estimates which have little basis in reality.
Indeed, officials of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs have estimated the savings due to continued limited compulsory licensing would have been about $166 million in 1983 if Bill C-22 had been in effect since 1969. This estimate uses the same criteria as that used by Dr. Eastman in his report. However, the drug prices review board would have added between $60 million and $200 million in additional savings to the savings from modified compulsory licensing. There will therefore be a net saving to consumers by monitoring the prices of all prescription drugs.
The Government has taken great care to design a pharmaceutical policy that will result in the maximum benefit for Canada and for Canadians. I am very confident that Bill C-22 as it was passed by this House on May 6 incorporates every element needed for this to happen.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member several questions. First, why does he take the advice of the multinational drug companies as to what will happen instead of listening to organizations representing a majority of Manitobans? These organizations have indicated very clearly
Patent Act
their opposition to this Bill. 1 refer him to the positions taken by the Manitoba Organization of Seniors, the Manitoba Federation of Labour, the Manitoba section of the Consumers' Association of Canada, and an organization with which he should have very close contact, Keystone Agriculture, an organization which represents all the farm commodity groups in Manitoba. Keystone Agriculture has expressed its opposition to this Bill as well.
Six provinces have now joined that opposition. All of those provinces have pharmacare programs under which the provinces pay all or a substantial part of the prescription-drug costs of their residents. All of them have made it very clear that they have looked at the figures and done their estimates and that the cost to their programs will be increased very substantially.
Second, does the Hon. Member not realize that the drug prices review board will have very little power to do anything about prices since the vast majority of prescription drugs will be produced in the countries in which they are researched including the United States, Switzerland and Great Britain? Does he not realize that the transfer prices they charge their Canadian subsidiaries have no relationship at all to the real cost of the drug? They can charge anything they want to their Canadian subsidiaries which will be packaging the drugs and the drug prices review board will not be able to have any say about that at all. It will have no way of determining whether or not the real price is being charged to the Canadian manufacturers.

In committee, we asked them-

I sat here quietly while you asked your question. I would appreciate the same respect. I asked the Hon. Member in committee for some proof of where these figures came from, and found that they had no basis in fact. They were pulled out of the air. It cannot be proven where they come from.

Opposition Members have been preying on the fears of these poor people.
In his speech on Friday, the Minister mentioned several of the groups and experts who feel that Bill C-22 will be beneficial to consumers and to the health care of Canadians. He mentioned the Medical Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Science Council of Canada, Dr. Michel

Chretien, the Clinical Research Institute and the Canadian Association of Retired Persons. I could spend 10 minutes listing the groups and experts who believe this Bill will be beneficial.
The Hon. Member's second question dealt with the drug prices review board. The Hon. Member said that it will have very little power. I submit that under our present system, 93 per cent of drugs in Canada have absolutely no price restrictions. They can be priced at any amount. There is no way that we can regulate or control those prices. I would think the Hon. Member would welcome a system that will try to keep those prices down.
Dr. Eastman who headed the commission back in 1983 will head the board. He is optimistic that it will be effective in controlling prices. Rather than being such a pessimist, I would think the Hon. Member would say that he approves of the Bill, let us try it for four years so that we may control the prices of these 93 per cent of drugs which do not attract generic competitors. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, who in most circumstances is a very sensible man, has spoken about opposition Members drawing figures from the air. By his own admission, the figures about the amount of money to be invested in research on which this legislation is based come from the air. Those figures come from a promise.
Even that promise amounts to very little because, as has been pointed out, if one projects expenditures by the pharmaceutical industry between now and 1995 based on trend lines already established, they would be at about the level promised by those who are trying to gain support for this legislation. Many figures are drawn from the air, but they are not drawn from the air by members of the New Democratic Party or those who are in opposition to the legislation. They are drawn from the air by those who support it.
We have heard a great deal about research and development. I know that the Hon. Member, being a sensible man, a well informed man and a fair man, would have taken the time to investigate thoroughly what amount of money promised, within that limited context I described before, will really go to basic research. I do not mean clinical trials nor do I mean researching new packaging for pills, new colours or something that will make medications more palatable. I mean basic research, the kind of research that will lead to new discoveries about the mechanisms by which viruses affect cells. How much research will there be into nerve transmission mechanisms? How much fundamental research will be done in the way in which nucleic acids and proteins function and how those functions become disturbed? How much research will there be into the understanding of that disturbance, making it possible to design drugs on a well-informed, scientific basis? What guarantee is there that the promise will be kept that there will be great breakthroughs through investment by multinational corporations who have their centres elsewhere?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked about figures coming out of the air. As far as the Government is concerned, the $800 million figure has not come out of the air, it has been coming out of the air waves. These companies have made the commitment. If the Member would study the Bill he will see there is a four year review and teeth in the Bill to deal with those companies which have not met their commitments. As to the figures 1 used about the saving resulting from the drug prices review board, we used the same criteria and the same basket of drugs used by Dr. Eastman in his report and plugged in Bill C-22 as if it had been in effect from 1969 through 1983. We did not pull those figures from the air. It is using his criteria, his formula, and the figures are accurate.
As to research, clinical versus basic, I know from the industry that clinical research in pharmaceuticals is very important. Some very important discoveries have been made. Basic research is important but in the pharmaceutical and biotech industry, clinical research is very important. I cannot predict what the breakdown will be, but I can give three quick examples of what compulsory licensing has done to drive our scientists out of Canada.
I was speaking to a researcher at the St. Boniface Hospital in Winnipeg who told me about two researchers at the University of Manitoba who discovered two new compounds and packed their bags and left the country to develop them further because of our compulsory licensing laws. A scientist in Ontario developed a naturally occurring substance which lowered blood pressure. This was a major breakthrough. He packed up his bags and moved out of the country because of our compulsory licensing system. Those are the people we want to keep in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pride and pleasure that I rise today to speak to the House of Commons as the representative of the people of the constituency of St. John's East.

Mr. Speaker, I am proud and pleased today to address Members of the House of Commons on behalf of the people of St. John's East.
I intend to improve my knowledge of French to be more at ease when addressing this House.

It is of great significance to me that my first full speech in the House of Commons deals with a Bill such as this. I believe there is a lesson for all Newfoundlanders in this Bill and the actions of the Government. I was born six months before the Confederation of Newfoundland and Canada in 1949. I am very conscious that I am here as a Newfoundlander as well as a Canadian to fight to ensure that all Newfoundlanders get their fair and just share of the fruits of this great nation. I am also here to ensure that they get a fair and equal opportunity to use their talents and energy to better themselves, their families and their country.
For several hundred years before we became part of Canada the people of the communities of St. John's East struggled against a harsh and demanding environment in order to make a living, mostly from the sea in the great fishing and sealing industries which existed off our coasts and in Labrador. They also struggled against their economic masters, the great fish merchants of the west country of England, the multinationals of their day, and the fish merchants of Newfoundland, their local counterparts. The fish merchants determined the price they would pay fishermen for their fish. These same merchants often being the only source of supply, would also decide the price of food and other supplies sold to fishermen. This system benefited the few and neglected and kept down the many. As a consequence of this economic relationship. Governments of Newfoundland have also been in a position of subservience to other countries and other interests.
While Canada was experiencing a level of maturity constitutionally in 1931, Newfoundland was going through a very severe economic period. In its relationship with the mother country, as England was then known, the Newfoundland Government, not the people of Newfoundland, gave in to its

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
demands to give up self-government. Newfoundland had selfgovernment for 100 years. In 1933, it gave up self-government as a result of the recommendations and demands made upon it by the international financial community.
In 1949, Newfoundlanders joined in Confederation with Canada. That was done with the hope that being a part of the great nation of Canada we would together be able to create our own destiny, decide our own future and determine our own priorities. What we now have before this Elouse is legislation which is a direct counter to that.
The people of Canada have spoken about this Bill. Since 1969 we have had legislation and a format for the control and availability of drugs which was the envy of other parts of the world. Drug prices in Canada, compared to those in the U.S., improved considerably as a result of that legislation. A report prepared by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs showed that in 1969, drug prices were 9 per cent higher in Canada than in the U.S. In 1976, they were 21 per cent lower than in the U.S. That shows that the legislation created the opportunity for generic drug companies to make available to Canadians in need these beneficial drugs at a lower price.
We have also heard much talk about employment and jobs flowing from the legislation before us. During a similar period, that is 1967 to 1982, employment in the drug industry in Canada rose by 28.8 per cent. In the U.S. during that same time, when they enjoyed the absence of compulsory licensing, employment rose by 22 per cent. So we have a decrease in drug prices and an increase in employment in Canada during that period.
Given these facts, how can we explain why the Government brought in legislation that turns the benefits of the 1969 legislation around and goes back to what we had before? How do we explain the fact that it makes available to the multinational drug companies a monopoly on the use of patents for drugs necessary to the health of Canadians?
As a newcomer to the legislature I made it my business to do research and prepare for this speech. I found out a number of interesting things. Perhaps I will bore the House with a certain bit of naivety. There is a history of efforts by the multinational drug corporations to influence the Government of Canada. It appears to have been very successful. It goes back to a very powerful cartel of multinational drug companies which, over the last 15 years, have attacked the generic companies in Canada and the United States. These companies have stopped at nothing in attacking generic drug companies.
I have before me a report contained in Consumer Reports of August of this year entitled "The big lie about generic drugs." This is the big lie being promoted by the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association in the United States. This comprehensive article says that with increased competition in sight from generics in the United States, beginning in 1983 the
major pharmaceutical firms opened a campaign of disparagement, which continues to this day, confusing and frightening doctors, pharmacists and patients alike. When Ayerst Laboratories, which operates in Canada as well as the United States, realized that it would soon face competition from a generic version of its drug called Inderal, a hypertension drug which was one of its most profitable drugs bringing in sales in excess of $350 million per year, it started a propaganda campaign aimed at both doctors and pharmacists.
It told doctors that one ought to use Inderal because of its proven therapeutic efficiency, but that with the generic alternative the chance existed that the patient's response may be compromised. It warned the doctors of the possibilities of law suits from patients. They sent a letter to pharmacists discussing pharmacists' potential liability if the cheaper generic version were dispensed instead of Inderal. The letter warned of troublesome, expensive lawsuits which would generate adverse publicity.
The Food and Drug Administration in the United States called this false and misleading. It said it served only to confuse and intimidate pharmacists into dispensing only Inderal. This is the kind of activity these companies undertake in order to discredit generic drug companies. It is reported that pharmaceutical manufacturers spend approximately $9,000 per doctor per year to convince them to use their drugs. This is an incredible amount of money to be spending on propaganda and promotion of drugs.
It is not surprising that these companies have supporters within the medical profession in these debates. These companies attempt to promote their drugs by taking doctors on trips to introduce them to their new drugs. Various other perks are granted to physicians in order to induce them to be sympathetic to the drug industry.
I am sure the House is well aware that as part of this campaign the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association took the opportunity to lobby intensively the Government of Canada, Members of Parliament, officials of the Department and Ministers. The former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Ms. Judy Erola, said that the war got absolutely furious, that the lobbying was perhaps the strongest she had ever seen. Ms. Erola replaced the previous Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), who was pushing for changes in the drug legislation as a result of lobbying efforts.
As of March 30 of this year, Ms. Erola became the President of the Pharmaceutical Manufacturers Association of Canada. The most formidable and strongest lobby that the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs had ever seen had found a spokesperson in Ms. Erola after she ceased to be the Minister.
In bowing to the wishes of the multinational corporations the Government is assisting these corporations to increase their massive profits. The profits of these companies are, by any measure, outrageous. On January 6 of this year, the Globe and
August 24, 1987

Mail reported that shareholders could be in line for a bonanza from major pharmaceutical companies which, cash rich from drug sale profits, were buying back their own shares and considering an increase in dividends.
"The major reason for the growing generosity of pharmaceutical concerns toward their shareholders is that they are sitting on piles of excess cash from their booming business. Some of those funds amount to more than $1 billion, which can be a drag on the balance sheet in the current low growth, low interest rate environment." The excess $1 billion which is lying around is a drag on the balance sheet. These are the kinds of profits which these multinational drug companies have lying around and must do something with.
In the United States they are recognizing Canada's example in controlling the use of new drug discoveries. Henry Waxman is the chairman of the Subcommittee on Health and Environment of the United States House of Representatives Committee on Energy and Commerce which conducted hearings into the issue of drug prices and generic drugs. His subcommittee issued a report showing that prescription drug prices in the United States increased more than 79 per cent during the past six years. The industry had spent only one out of every three dollars of that increase on research and development. But the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) is asking us to give the industry more money, which we will not recover in research and development. All we have is a promise and nothing else.
The Hon. Member for Dauphin-Swan River (Mr. White) referred to the Minister of Consumer Affairs for Manitoba of acting like a political opportunist when he opposed the legislation. I ask the Hon. Member if he considered the Minister of Consumer Affairs and the Minister of Health for the Province of Newfoundland to have acted as political opportunists when they criticized the Government of Canada for its legislation?
The people of Newfoundland were told for many years by the Party in power in Newfoundland that when we the Newfoundland Provincial Government and the federal Government are of the same political persuasion, we will see the kind of development Newfoundland needs to take its rightful place in Confederation. The Minister of Consumer Affairs of the Province of Newfoundland advised members of the committee that in June of 1985, he was first presented with the federal proposals to amend the Patent Act. At that time he outlined the province's concern that they would have a significant impact on drug prices in Canada, especially in Newfoundland and Labrador. On May 22, 1986, he wrote to the then Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs advising him of his Government's strong opposition to the federal Government's plans to amend the Patent Act.
There were further proposals given later to the Government in June, and in September when they were again discussed, the
Patent Act
Government of Newfoundland considered the argument put forward by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. After consideration, the Government of Newfoundland would still not support the amendments. The concern expressed was for the impact on the consumer due to the expected drug price increases, and the lack of commitment of the federal Government to any definite job creation and business development plans for the Province of Newfoundland as a result of these amendments.
The Parliamentary Secretary for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said in the House this afternoon that there is nothing we can do except have faith in the promises-

landed on the shores, so to speak, and announced that if this Bill were passed, all kinds of jobs in research and development would be created in Nova Scotia for young people. Mr. Speaker, of course I am tremendously pleased to rise today in this important debate on Bill C-22. As a Quebecer and a Canadian, 1 would like that we assume once more our rightful place in the research and development of pharmaceuticals. I do not want to see another flight of foreign capital away from that industry. I do not want to see any more our young university graduates having to go abroad when our education system and their parents spent a lot of money so that they could study in our universities right here in Canada. Let us be realistic- when we invest, we want that investment to yield a return. It is rather embarrassing that a large country like Canada, exporting as it does 80 percent of its goods to other nations, does not protect the inventions of our Quebecers, our researchers, our scientists.
Quebecers understand that, except that I wonder if the New Democrats, the Liberals who are sitting here today-I think that some are from Quebec but they were not here when the
Patent Act
time came to vote. The others do not know Quebec. They claim to know Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you right now that although I speak some English, I do not claim to know Ontario. But I do know Quebec and I know what is good for Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer to an editorial by Jean-Guy Dubuc that appeared in La Presse, from which I would like to quote one paragraph if I may:
Only Liberal Senators did not understand what is at stake in the debate. Even Quebec senators are willing to forget Quebec's interests in order to defend those of Ontario. It is not surprising that the Senators have even convinced the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. John Turner, who supports them without seeming to know-or perhaps knowing only too well-that the Liberal Government had promised the Quebec Government to amend the legislation when Mr. Andre Ouellet was Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Now, Quebecers and all Canadians will have to pay the price of the Liberal vendettas.
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very glad to see the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) in the House. I had the pleasure of sitting with him on the Special Committee on Parliamentary Reform. I can tell you that I learned much from him on that committee. He has a lot of experience, knowledge and common sense. 1 think that he will be speaking after me, perhaps to tell his colleagues in the Senate and even on the other side of the House to take some tranquilizers and get a bit of rest.
As a matter of fact, since we know that some Senators like to sleep outside the Senate Chamber, it would perhaps not be a bad idea for all the Liberals to take tranquilizers and go to sleep at the door of the Senate. The Senators could-

Mr. Speaker, I am greatful to you for calling me to order and asking me to show respect to the Upper House. In this case, 1 will be so to speak respectful, Mr. Speaker.
To return to what I was saying concerning my friend from Papineau, Mr. Speaker, I will certainly remain until the end of his speech, because I am sure that, as a sensible man, he will tell his colleagues that the infusion of $1.4 billion would create nearly 3,000 jobs over the next ten years. I suggest that because of his habitual eloquence, the Hon. Member for Papineau and former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will make an extraordinary speech in support of the Government and its Bill C-22.
Mr. Speaker, it is also suggested that the Senate report which is here before the House would not succeed in stopping the brain drain. Thousands of students and scientists would

August 24, 1987
Patent Act
continue to leave Canada to seek opportunities elsewhere. It is too bad!
Mr. Speaker, if 1 were a parent today-unfortunately, I never had children, something I regret-and if my children were attending university, and studying pure science, I would ask mysel serious questions. I might suggest to them to make another option, because the opportunities for promotion in Canada are few and far between.
Mr. Speaker, my Argenteuil-Papineau constituents whom I was pleased to meet all summer long do not quite understand. As you know, not everyone can boast of knowing our Parliamentary system. It is difficult for someone to understand how come we on this side of the House, who are the elected government, are not capable with 211 Members to pass a piece of legislation. You know the average citizen wonders why, and this is the reason why for a number of years we have been talking of reforming the Senate, which I respect as you suggested 1 should do.
Mr. Speaker, the Senate's proposals jeopardize all the efforts made by this Government to change the structure of the Canadian pharmaceutical industry. If adopted, the Senate's proposals would mean that pharmaceutical firms would keep on importing from abroad the active ingredients and simply mix them, or even import the final product and only do clinical tests in order to comply with the requirements of National Health and Welfare.
Mr. Speaker, the exclusivity periods proposed by the Senate make no distinction between pharmaceuticals that are entirely invented and manufactured in Canada and products that are simply imported. The Senate's proposals now before us do not do any good on any count. They do not stimulate research activities or grant adequate protection to Canadian innovators.
Mr. Speaker, this Government has a duty to afford special protection under Bill C-22 to pharmaceuticals that are invented and manufactured in Canada, and this for a number of good reasons. First, it is a matter of fairness to inventors.
Mr. Speaker, if I was an inventor-or should I say an "inventress"-I would be frustrated at not being able to do any research. I would be frustrated at having studied in our great Canadian and Quebec universities but not being in a position to use my knowledge for my own country-the country that gave me those vital instruments, our universities-and at not being able to contribute to the progress of that country. We must afford the same degree of protection to inventions in the pharmaceutical industry as to any other invention, Mr. Speaker. Drugs are an basic necessity and we must therefore do all in our power to protect and reward investigators who develop drugs which improve the quality of life of all Canadian men and women.
Mr. Speaker, as one prominent journalist put it: it is well worth two or three cents more a pill. Yes, it is well worth it!
Secondly, affording better protection to drugs invented and developed here in Canada is a stimulus to fundamental
research since it is here that investigators must initiate the discovery process. That is how we could make the Canadian pharmaceutical industry a major field of innovation.
My friend the Hon. Member for Papineau (M. Ouellet) represents a riding located in the Montreal area, Mr. Speaker, one from which foreign capital has fled to other provinces and even to other countries. This is because people believed that our Quebec language legislation, Bil 101, would be detrimental to business interests.
Mr. Speaker, in an aside I must say that it would be awful if the New Democrats came to power. The Montreal economy is just beginning to recover. Just try to imagine, Mr. Speaker, what we would look like if the New Democrats, with their way of thinking, were to say no to free trade and did not want to protect the wonderful opportunity the Bill before the House affords our researchers.
Mr. Speaker, with such a protection for drugs invented and developed here, how could Canada not attract capital investment as well as manufacturing facilities? Companies which will invest in Canada will be able to recover their costs adequately. We must also remember that our Canadian researchers will be strongly encouraged to stay in Canada instead of leaving our country to go to our main trade partners.
Mr. Speaker, a researcher, an inventor who works for a large manufacturing company, particularly a drug manufacturer, earns quite a lot of money. He is not a low income earner. He is well paid. It means that this man who is involved in research and his family contribute directly to other important sectors of our economy. They are good consumers who support other small and medium businesses around them. So if all these great scientists with big earnings leave to go where it is financially and intellectually more rewarding, the loser is not only the drug industry, but the whole regional economy.
For a long time, scientific groups doing research in Canada have been hoping for a Bill which would encourage Canadian discoveries. They were not the only ones, Mr. Speaker. I wonder how caucus members can be against the premier of their own province, against all the ministers from the province of Quebec that we represent in Ottawa, against all the companies which probably contributed to our election, whichever side we are on, how can they be against all these people? I wonder.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, most of the medical discoveries done in our universities and research institutes are bought by foreign companies which develop commercially products invented in Canada. This is a shameful and unacceptable situation which has to be changed.
Our Prime Minister said we should do something and we did, Mr. Speaker. The proposals of the Upper Chamber bring us back to a situation which had been denounced with the utmost vigor by our best scientists.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, a country which wants to be at the leading edge of technology . . . You will recall that three or
August 24, 1987

four years ago the Premier of Quebec said: "We are living in a period of technological change. We have to face the music." The time when Canada was only able to sell to its American neighbor is over. We have now access to much larger markets. Think of the nations of Asia and the Pacific, Mr. Speaker. Here is a very interesting market. Mr. Speaker, consider all the potential investments if, as a nation, we are intelligent enough to protect the intellectual property of our researchers as well as the inventions of the companies.
Mr. Speaker, it stands to reason that if in any field ... Consider for instance our designers in the clothing sector, our designers in other commercial undertakings. Very few people like to have their ideas copied by others. Somebody spends a fortune to come up with a new product, it has hardly been marketed and practically overnight others are producing copies. If 1 were an investor in that field, you can understand why I would not be in too much of a hurry to get my money out of the bank to invest more. On the contrary, I would be tempted to go and see what is happening elsewhere, which is exactly what others did. They invested elsewhere.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I emphasize the fact that Canada has every right to rank first in pharmaceutical research and that our researchers are entitled to more protection for anything they invent in this country.
Bill C-22 confirms this, and any amendment which could be made would deny these rights.
Mr. Speaker, I strongly hope that everyone will be sensible, that our friends in the Upper and Lower Chambers, in front of us and beside us will sleep peacefully, read everything that has been said, listen to everything, and change their minds. We changed our minds ourselves in the past because Canadiens told us that we had perhaps gone a bit too far. Canadians are now saying that the Senators and our Liberal and NDP friends opposite are going too far about Bill C-22. It is now time to be reasonable and to approve Bill C-22, Mr. Speaker.
