Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part today in this debate on Bill C-22 dealing with drug patents. I am all the more so because, while I was Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in 1983, the Liberal Government of the time had looked into this very complex and important issue. I must say that the Members of this House and the other place who belong to the Liberal Party have never declared themselves against changes to the current legislation. As a matter of fact, we were the first to propose a review of the present system. The recommendations which appear in the Eastman Report, an independent commission created by the former Government to find out about what is true and false in
this area, seem to us to be quite reasonable, because they set a balance between the interests of consumers and the need to increase research within the pharmaceutical industry.
Unfortunately, 1 have to say that once more the Conservative Government has chosen to be overly generous with the Americans.
Recently we were told by General Motors that this Government had made them an offer they could not refuse for keeping their plant in operation in St. Therese. In other words, from what General Motors told us, they had the choice either to stay in St. Therese or to close the plant. But the Government offer was so generous that they were left with no choice. They took the money and stayed.
It is precisely this kind of generosity with the Americans that once again we are blaming the Conservative Government for with regard to pharmaceutical products.
As Liberals, we are not against changing the law. However, we object to undue concessions to pharmaceutical companies.
The Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) has quite a list of questions put together by the department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to be asked of those who participate in this debate. But when asked a while ago, what kind of safeguards had been obtained with regard to investments and jobs, the Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) preferred to remain silent in her seat. Because there are really no safeguards. The Member for Portneuf can goof-off all he wants behind the curtains, but if he has any proof, it should be tabled in the House. We will listen to him and even applaud him. Except that he has absolutely no proof that the multinationals will make the required investments.
We feel the Government chose to go much further than Professor Eastman's recommendations. It chose to tilt the scales in favour of the multinational pharmaceutical corporations, to the detriment of the Canadian generic drugs industry and Canadian consumers. We feel this is deplorable because fundamentally, what we Liberals have always been striving for is a balance between the real and pressing need for increased drug research and the corresponding need that those drugs be made available at prices that people can afford, and this we have a duty to ensure.
This is why we are supporting the Eastman Report's recommendations and this is why we, Liberal Members in this House, are of one mind with Liberal Senators who want to amend the bill to guarantee that the investments promised by the multinational corporations take place, that the jobs promised are created, and also that prices remain at levels that consumers can afford.
And that position of course is different from that of the New Democratic Party who want no change-they want the status quo. Of course, the short term status quo as supported by the New Democratic Party might be of benefit to consumers, but it would provide no incentive for the drug industry to develop new drugs.
August 24, 1987

But we say: Drug companies are willing to invest, they are ready to create jobs. Hurrah! Let us use that opportunity, let us amend the act. But let us not be blind to the point of thinking that drug corporations will deliver all the goods if we do not have a legislation with teeth. And unfortunately, the current bill does not provide the formal guarantees we are hoping for. And there lies the basic difference between the government's position and ours. We agree that the act has to be amended, but we believe the government is going too far when making a 10-year concession to the drug corporations- that is excessive in our view. The Eastman Report recommends four years and a 14 percent royalty. Obviously, those who engage in research, those who invest considerable amounts to put a new product on the market must meet their costs. It is absolutely essential that, in order to continue bringing new products onto the market, pharmaceutical firms be afforded a degree of protection which allows them to meet their costs and turn a reasonable profit. The Eastman Report tells us, based on an objective, in-depth evaluation of the issue, that four years are enough protection to allow the drug industry multinationals not only to meet their costs but to attain reasonable returns on their investment. So what does the Government do rather than leave it at four years? It gives them ten years. In other words, pharmaceutical firms are given an extra six years which, we contend, is based on no good reason and is not justified.
This situation is of great concern to us since we know that at the Irish Summit, the 1985 meeting between the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and the President of the United States, President Reagan had insisted that Canadian patent legislation be harmonized with American legislation before the initiation of the free trade negociations. We also know that Mr. Clayton Yeutter, President Reagan's trade adviser, has stated that he would suspend the free trade talks if Canada did not honour its committment to give better patent protection to American multinationals.
And finally, we know that the American pharmaceutical industry had in hand a preliminary version of the bill we are now studying, Bill C-22, even before it was tabled in this House. What we are saying then is that the Conservative Government has caved in to the influential American lobby, that the bill in its present form goes too far and is far too generous for the pharmaceutical industry.
And there is no better proof of that than to recall that in the first version of the bill as tabled by the former Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Hon. Member for Langeiier (Mr. Cote), there was a provision intended to encourage inventors of patented products to manufacture them in Canada whereby they would be protected only if the drugs were manufactured in Canada. And so what happened between the first and second versions? That clause has vanished.
I see that you are preparing to put an end to the debate. I would simply want to quote the following from the document

It disappeared. And in our opinion, it is more evidence of the Conservatives' submission, their kowtowing to American interests.

speechtext:
that Bill C-223, an Act to amend the Official Languages Act (primacy of the Act), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part today in a debate on a bill I introduced on October 14, 1986 and which is one of a series of bills I tabled in the House over the last ten years or so.
Bill C-223 we are considering tonight seeks to recognize the primacy of the Official Languages Act, to make that Act supreme over any other statute. I am introducing that Bill because the matter is important, Mr. Speaker, knowing full well that in a bill tabled as recently as June 25, 1987 Hon. Members will have the opportunity to discuss this fall, 1 presume, the Government agrees to grant the Official Languages Act a qualified primacy, so to speak, but some primacy nonetheless over Canadian statutes, or the law of the land.
Today, Mr. Speaker, I will try to explain why the Official Languages Act should explicitly contain a clause that guarantees its primacy over all other legislation.
When the legislator includes the concept of primacy in an Act, he confers on this Act a quasi constitutional character because it is thereby clearly distinguished from other Acts while, as we know, remaining subject to amendment or repeal by the same legislative authority from which it received this primacy. The effect of primacy is to make the Act supersede any provisions of any other Act that are inconsistent with the former, unless otherwise stated. That was the purpose of Bill C-223, and that was also the purpose of many other Bills I shall not mention here but which have been considered in the House from time to time and, I must admit, have always been postponed indefinitely because, as I was told at the time, it was too much, too soon. Too much, too soon has become a very familiar refrain for people like me who have taken up the cause of official languages. We are always being told: You are in too much of a hurry and you are asking too much.
I must say that the Government-this Government did not originate the concept but it tabled the Bill and drafted it-1 must say that Bill C-72, which will be before the House for second reading in the fall, proposes that the primacy of this Act shall apply to the first five parts of the Bill in question. There are shortcomings and there are sections which I will certainly try to have amended in order to broaden the scope of the legislation and extend its primacy beyond what is being proposed, but on the whole, Mr. Speaker, we are pleased, and I am even quite satisfied with this major step forward embodied in Bill C-72.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps 1 should provide some brief historical notes in the few minutes I have at my disposal. As you know, the Official Languages Act was adopted in 1969, after an extensive national debate. It started with the B and B or Laurendau-Dunton Commission. At the time, the Commission went around the country, trying to find a way to resolve the crisis that was troubling Canadians, a crisis which, I hope, has now more or less died down, and I even hope it will disappear altogether.
But in a few minutes I will have the opportunity to remind you that even here in Ontario today we still experience difficulties when trying to make some people understand that the official languages of this country, English and French, do not in any way prevent either group from asserting its rights. Whether 1 do so in French or whether I do so in English does not take anything away from the other group: it can assert its rights in its own language. Francophones outside Quebec-and that includes me-assert their right to exist in French in Ontario, or in British Columbia for that matter, and I would hope that a country which claims to be basically bilingual, with two official languages, would show full respect for the aspirations of its minorities in the various provinces. This is sometimes difficult because it is not easy to defend oneself, to fight to have one's own schools, to have one's school rights recognized, to have one's rights respected before the courts, and to have one's rights in the legislative assembly.
Remember Alberta where an individual was denied the right to speak in his own language. Remember that before the courts today, in both Eastern and Western Canada, Canadians sometimes find it difficult to appear and give evidence in their own language, French, just as it has been difficult now and then for some anglophones in Quebec to understand and to be able to use their own language everywhere when they wanted to do so. Mr. Speaker, because of this ongoing evolution over the last 20 or 25 years, we now have today before us, after 18 years, a new piece of legislation containing what is in my opinion an important clause which asserts the primacy of the Act.
When the Official Languages Act was passed in 1969, it was a great step forward. For the first time in Canada, we recognized that we have two official languages, and implemented legislation to ensure the equality of English and French in federal parliamentary institutions.
August 24, 1987

While certain problems with the 1969 Act have come to light and brought the Government to introduce a new bill, Bill C-72, we must not forget that the 1969 Act has been the major instrument in changing public attitudes as concerns official languages.
It is because of the evolution in attitudes especially, and of the action taken by some Governments that the 1969 Act has become outmoded and needs to be brought up to date.
When the Liberal Government of the time adopted the Act in 1969, our Constitution had not yet been patriated. The rights of official languages minorities to be taught in their own language throughout Canada did not exist, neither did the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and so on.
While we say that the 1969 Act needed to be amended, this does not mean that the problems were identified by the Conservative Government. Since its passage in 1969, the Act has been examined in depth by the Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons and applied in all federal Departments. The Official Languages Commissioner examines how this is done and reports each year to Parliament.
It is by applying the Act and looking at the results that we were able to identify weaknesses. For instance, the concept of bilingual districts has never been implemented because it was restrictive and seemed unnecessary, while the language of work concept, which is vaguely defined in Section 2 of the Official Languages Act, quickly became one of the main problems with this legislation. The amendments to the Act have therefore been identified thanks mostly to the reports of the Joint Committee on Official Languages. Indeed, four of the main reports of this Committee contain recommendations for amendments to the 1969 Act. These are the first, fourth and fifth reports of the Thirty Second Parliament, tabled in July 1981, June 1982 and April 1983, as well as the second report of the Thirty Third Parliament tabled recently.
Given that Bill C-72 contains most of the proposed amendments, it would seem appropriate to sum them up in order to put this debate in context and give credit, in particular, to the joint committee which worked very hard and submitted amendments which I consider contructive and which will reinforce the Act.
The first report of 1981 proposed two changes, first the repeal of all clauses dealing with bilingual districts and second the inclusion in the Act of the expressions "where numbers warrant" and "active offer of services".
We should recall that 1981 was a year of constitutional negotiations. The reference to numbers comes from the desire to harmonize the Act and the constitutional document. As to the active offer of services it will be embodied in the Act of 1987, in Section 27.
The fourth report, in 1982, added three new subjects. First a section to clarify the question of the language of work, a recommandation made by the committee following contested decisions of the courts. I recognize that the Act of 1987 took
Official Languages Act
that into consideration since it defines the language of work and its application in Sections 33 and 34. But the Government did not invent anything, it merely reproduced the parliamentary resolution of 1973 on the language of work, passed by this House in June 1973.
Then, again to clarify the Act, following the courts' rulings, the committee recommended that it should be made binding and declaratory, which means it should contain provisions making its implementation compulsory. It would therefore establish rights-we could for instance before the courts ask for compliance with the Act. The 1987 Act implements part of that recommendation in Sections 75(1) and 76(1). I need only remind Hon. Members the issue of airline employees and the whole disruption that was brought about by the court ruling that Section 2 of the Official Languages Act was only declaratory and not binding. This caused us many problems and we are trying to amend and strengthen the legislation, as I said earlier, in order to make it binding and declaratory.
Finally, the Committee insisted on the inclusion of a section regarding the fair participation of both language groups in this country, which is covered by the preamble and Part VI of the 1987 Act, Bill C-72. As regards the fifth Report of the Committee, one of its main recommendations concerns the recognition of the supremacy of the law. To some people, that issue was settled by the fact that Sections 16 to 20 of the Charter of Rights were enshrined in the 1982 Constitution Act. In fact, as the Charter is enshrined in the Constitution, it will render inoperative those provisions that are inconsistent on any other rule of law, in view of the supremacy of the Constitution. Incidentally, the wording of the Charter is almost exactly the same as Section 2 of the 1969 Official Languages Act.
In other people's view, the law will always be the interpretation framework for judges who try to determine the spirit and the intent of the law. If the law is not specific enough, the very vague safeguards provided for in Section 16(1) of the Charter will prevail. There have been many court rulings to this effect. In fact, the Deputy Minister of Justice confirmed it when he appeared before the Committee in March, April and May 1982.
Thus, to protect the provisions of the Official Languages Act, it is essential to include a clause that clearly asserts the intent of the law to give that act precedence over any other act, order, decree, by-law, rule or regulation.
Mr. Speaker, these events summarize the evolution of the issue from 1969 to 1982, when the problem of the primacy of the Act was recognized and identified. I am not saying that this problem occurred all of a sudden in 1982. What I mean to say is that from 1969 to 1982, the issue was examined from every angle and the courts rendered their decisions. It is a long process of interpretation and identification of the problem, as well as determination of the remedy which has made the

August 24, 1987
Official Languages Act
primacy of the Act a central and even significant issue in Bill C-72 which was introduced by this Government.
Mr. Speaker, I was involved in various capacities in this process. As an Hon. Member, as a Member of the Committee on Official Languages, and as chairman of this Committee. As an Hon. Member, I introduced a number of private bills calling on the House to adopt the principle of the primacy of the Official Languages Act. In 1984, I introduced a couple of bills, including Bills C-203 and C-223, all of which were seeking to establish the primacy of the Official Languages Act, thereby giving it a quasi-constitutional character, since all other legislation had to be subordinated to it, just as ordinary legislation are subordinated to the Constitution.
1 do not want to repeat the need to establish the primacy of the Act, for I have dealt enough with it from the start, preferring to show how Bill C-223 would provide in some cases a better protection than the provisions of Bill C-72. For instance, Clause 1 of Bill C-223 provides for the implicit repeal of any provision of a law of Canada in case of conflict, unless the notwithstanding clause applied. Moreover, Clause 11(1) made it an obligation for the Minister of Justice to examine every regulation to ascertain whether any inconsistency existed. The primacy sought through Bill C-223 is aimed at the subject matter of the Official Languages Act and not at the whole legislation. More specifically, it is to Section 2 that this primacy should have been provided.
Clause 79 (1) of Bill C-72 provides also that the primacy of the Act will be limited to certain provisions of the legislation, more specifically Parts I to IV which supersede all conflicting provisions of any other federal legislation or regulation.
Such a procedure namely the reference to explicit rather than implicit content, as in the case of Bill C-223, has advantages as well as disadvantages. On the positive side, this difference will dispel some of the doubts felt by judges because they will know exactly what the legislator was referring to when he granted the primacy of the law. Conversely, this leaves no room for a wider interpretation by the courts. Thus, although Bill C-223 is general in its application and covers the Canadian Human Rights Act, section 79 (2) excludes it explicitly, and also excludes its rules. It so happens that in some sections of the Canadian Human Rights Act, for instance those providing that race, ethnic or national origin are grounds for discrimination, section 3 of the act, or section 7 concerning discrimination in hiring, and section 8 concerning job applications, advertising and, may very well, Mr. Speaker, contradict the Official Languages Act.
Linguistic rights could therefore be weakened due to the removal of discriminatory motives since the Canadian Human Rights Act is excluded from the primacy clause in Bill C-72.
Furthermore, the fact that Part VI in Bill C-72 is excluded from the paragraph concerning primacy could cause problems relating to representation, equal participation, language of work and language of service. For instance, there could be
conflicts between the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act and those of the Official Languages Act. If that were to be the case, the Courts probably would decide in favour of the Public Service Employment Act rather than the Official Languages Act, because there is a rule that an Act of specific scope takes precedence over an Act of general scope, as is the Official Languages Act, because it will be remembered that Justice Deschenes in the Gens de l'air case in 197778 ruled it was an Act of general scope.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I submit that the situation as regards the primacy of the Official Languages Act has changed a lot since Bill C-72 was put in place. As 1 just said, the latter includes very specific provisions as to the primacy of the Act. I am quite pleased about that, Mr. Speaker. However, any specific provision eventually includes loopholes because of its very specificity. This is why it is useful to have legislations of a more general scope that become interpretation cases allowing the Courts to enjoy more flexibility, to be more open-minded in interpreting the law. Such is the thrust of Bill C-223 now before us. While being of general scope, it could complement the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Official Languages Act.
Moreover, Bill C-223 includes provisions that are used-as I say, it charges the Minister of Justice with the responsibility to look at any proposed regulations.
For all those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I urge all Hon. Members in this House to support the Bill. I believe it is essential that we make two amendments to Bill C-72, and they are in Bill C-223-one to give primacy to the Act, and for which I hope 1 have the support of Hon. Members, and another to charge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) with the responsibility to review any regulations to ensure that there is no inconsistency with any act voted by this Parliament. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I thank all Hon. Members for their attention.

Mr. Speaker, the issue of the primacy of the Official Languages Act over conflicting rules in other Acts has been abundantly discussed in the past. Already, in 1978,
August 24, 1987

the then Commissioner of Official Languages advocated that primacy in his annual report. Subsequently, a series of bills much to the same effect were tabled, as it happened most of them by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier. Meanwhile, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms took effect. It enshrines the basic principles of the present Official Languages Act and gives them special status since they are encompassed in the supreme legislation of the country.
On April 24, 1986, during the second reading debate on the last of the bills introduced by the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier, Bill C-203, an Act to amend the Official Languages Act, which dealt also with the primacy of that act, the importance of the matter had been acknowledged to a large extent. However, it was also emphasized a debate on this complex matter would not be appropriate at that time. Let me borrow from the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin), my colleague on this side of the House and co-chairman of the Standing Joint committee on Official languages, the words he said then, and I quote:
-it would be premature at this stage to go the supremacy route alone, since in-depth studies undertaken by the Ministers most involved in language reform, at the request of the Prime Minister, should very soon result in a number of proposals that will allow for consideration of all aspects involving the Act and its application.
As you know, that examination has been undertaken, the work has been done and we now have the pleasure of having before us a complete bill on the official languages. Bill C-72 gives meaning to our linguistic duality, covers all important aspects in the language field and provides us with a strong and durable legal base. It applies to all Canadians irrespective of their ethnic background or mother tongue, and whether they belong to a majority or a minority. It shows a strong will on the part of the Government to bring about a true and profound renewal of our language policy. It dovetails with our commitment of national reconciliation. In short, it has, I believe, all the necessary elements to answer the expectations of Canadians in this regard, even those of my friend from Ottawa- Vanier. In fact, that Bill on official languages provides, in Section 79, for the primacy of the main clauses of the Act over those in other federal Acts or Regulations that might be inconsistent with them. And that is not all.
In the administration of justice, it guarantees better access to federal courts by reasserting and defining the right of a defendant to use one or the other official language. The Bill also provides for a better access of the public to federal institutions by strengthening the right of Canadians to communicate with and receive services from these institutions in the language of their choice.
As to the language of work in federal institutions, the Bill specifies, for the first time, the right of federal civil servants to use either one of the two official languages at work. Moreover, the Government commits itself, in that Bill, to guaranteeing equal opportunities of employment and promotion in federal institutions to all Canadians, regardless of their ethnic
Official Languages Act
background or mother tongue, and to seeking in these institutions a distribution of staff which reflects the distribution in Canada of English-speaking and French-speaking communities.
As for the Francophone and Anglophone minorities in Canada, the Government is determined to promote their development. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to underline once again the Meech Lake Accord which recognizes the distinct character of Quebec. If we want to engage in an exercise in semantics, we all know that the specific character of Quebec means its language. The Secretary of State will play a major role in this regard as his mission will be to coordinate federal efforts in this area, for instance through co-operation with the provinces and the private and voluntary sectors.
The position of the Official Languages Commissioner will be maintained. His role will still be to ensure that the spirit and letter of the Act are respected, but he will have more effective tools at his disposal.
Finally, one of the major strengths of this Bill is the provision of legal redress. Those Canadians who feel that their linguistic rights have been violated can take their case to the Federal Court. This Bill is good for both French and English Canadians. This cannot be overemphasized. The Official Languages Commissioner will also have the possibility of legal recourse.
Mr. Speaker, one man who deserves credit for the introduction of Bill C-72 is the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
We have as Prime Minister someone who is completely and perfectly at ease in both official languages of our country. It is rare for a Prime Minister to master completely both official languages. I am proud to be a member of his team.
I believe that these few words are enough to show that Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada, is a major piece of legislation which the House will soon be able to examine. We can easily conclude that the Bill introduced by my Government on June 25 both encompasses and surpasses that introduced by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier. I therefore believe, Mr. Speaker, that, for the moment, there is no need to proceed further with consideration of Bill C-223 and that my Hon. friend for Ottawa-Vanier should certainly have made this clear and should perhaps simply have asked, as others have done before, that his Bill be withdrawn, as the Government has tabled a Bill which meets more than adequatly and even more substantially all the aspirations of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier, who is a great defender of the French language in the beautiful province of Ontario.

This is one of the best examples of a Member of Parliament, working in co-operation with the joint standing committee concerned with a special issue, in this case the primacy of the Official Languages Act, being persistent. As my hon. friend across the way indicated at the beginning of her speech, for many, many years the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier has put forward arguments year after year about the need to move in this direction, along with others in the House. He has done so once again in Bill C-223.
As a result of his persistence and as a result of his constantly reminding Parliament and his colleagues of the need to move on the whole matter of official language primacy, the Government in its wisdom has introduced Bill C-72. On June 25, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) introduced for first reading Bill C-72, an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada. That Bill is really a major step forward. Again, I think it is important at the outset that we indicate very clearly that these particular initiatives, Bill C-72 and Bill C-223, are of no threat to anyone in our country. They are a complement to Anglophones and Francophones. They are complements in terms of enhancing the status and role of those who wish to speak English and those who wish to speak French, or both, in Canada. Therefore it is a clear indication of the maturity and maturation that our country is going through to begin serious consideration of Bill C-72 sometime this fall.
I want to take off my hat, figuratively speaking, to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier for once again reminding us through Bill C-223 of the importance of establishing the primacy of the Official Languages Act. Establishing primacy is like giving a quasi-constitutional status to the Official Languages Act in that it will take precedence over other statutes. Other laws will be subordinate to it when it comes to matters of language.
When one recalls the passionate and thoughtful debate that occurred in 1969 when the Official Languages Act was originally passed, one will recall that all sides of the House felt strongly about this issue and believed that it was certainly in the best interests of Canada. Now, through the establishment of primacy of the Official Languages Act, I think we will advance the cause and therefore make very clear in all parts of the country how seriously we feel about the primacy and role of English and French in Canada. We still have some way to go.
As my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier indicated, not long ago in the Province of Alberta a Member of that Legislature, the Member from Lac La Biche, Mr. Leo Piquette, rose in the House and asked a question, through the Speaker, in French. In a sense he was chastised for that particular act. There has been a great deal of debate following that action in terms of the appropriateness of that particular move. What it did was to place on the public agenda discussion of the issue and, again, to advance the cause. We have learned from that. From what I can gather, the matter is now before the Legislature of
Alberta. Out of that will come a reasoned debate and, hopefully, a reasoned decision.
I do not want to belabor this point but I think that it would be appropriate to take a moment or two to refer to Bill C-72. I do this out of no disrespect for my colleague regarding Bill C-223. 1 believe that his Private Members' initiative which resulted in the introduction of Bill C-72 will see the real discussion and debate probably in a legislative committee or, perhaps, in a reference to a joint standing committee of the House of Commons and the Senate.
Bill C-72 is an Act respecting the status and use of the official languages of Canada. For our purposes this afternoon I will simply read the purpose of the Act since it would be appropriate for those listening and watching. The purpose of the Act is the following:
-to extend the present laws of Canada relating to official languages to
(a)	ensure respect for English and French as the official languages of Canada and ensure equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all federal institutions, in particular with respect to their use in parliamentary proceedings, in legislative and other instruments, in the administration of justice, in communicating with or providing services to the public and in carrying out the work of federal institutions;
(b)	support the development of English and French linguistic minority communities and generally advance the equality of status and use of the English and French languages within Canadian society; and
(c)	set out the powers, duties and functions of federal institutions with respect to the official languages of Canada.
In terms of a purpose that is, obviously, a laudatory purpose. As the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier has indicated, his Bill actually advances in some cases Bill C-72. It goes beyond what Bill C-72 covers. For that reason, his mentioning those areas in his Bill today will assist us in improving Bill C-72 when it comes forward for second reading and for discussion and amendment in legislative committee.
I am pleased to be part of the process that now works toward the establishment of the primacy of the Official Languages Act. It will set to rest a great deal of concern and wonderment that we have seen in the past when it was asked what, in fact, did take primacy, the Official Languages Act or some other statute. This, along with the passage not so much of Bill C-223 but the eventual passage of Bill C-72, will solve that issue once and for all.

Mr. Speaker, I think this is quite clear and that it would be very hard to misinterpret this clause. I would like to mention at this point that Bill C-72 was tabled in the House of Commons by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) and given first reading on June 25 of this year. This first provision of Bill C-72 is mentioned more specifically in Clause 2, and here again I will quote in English because I only have the English text:

"to extend the present laws of Canada relating to official languages".

This means that this legislation, Bill C-72, will reinforce all pertinent legislation to ensure that both official languages are

August 24, 1987
Official Languages Act
used by the Canadian Government and Parliament in their general administration and all their instruments,
Mr. Speaker, the same Bill contains a provision that is quite clear and which I will not translate but I would like to quote it to remind people of the full impact of Bill C-72. It reads as follows, and I quote:

-ensure respect for English and French as the official languages of Canada and ensure equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all federal institutions, in particular with respect to their use in parliamentary proceedings, in legislative and other instruments, in the administration of justice, in communicating with or providing services to the public and in carrying out the work of federal institutions.

Mr. Speaker, after sitting a number of times on the Official Languages Committee, 1 realize that it is still a fairly difficult business, especially for French Canadians, to ensure that while certain laws may be favoured by the majority of Canadians and thus compliance may not seem as problematic, nevertheless we must not forget that although the minority may not have numerical clout, it does have equal status and that we have two official languages in Canada. Let me explain, Mr. Speaker. The aim is to ensure that the status of both official languages is complete and that we, French Canadians, both outside and inside Quebec, may use the French language in total security, just as English speaking persons would be ensured the opportunity to speak in committee, in a committee that would be held in Montreal or Saint-Polycarpe or Saint-Telesphore or anywhere in Quebec, even if the majority is French-speaking, at that point, Canadians can speak both on Parliament matters and on Government matters or on any of its acts or regulations in the language of their choice.
Mr. Speaker, it is understood that the very clear intent of parts I to V is indeed to ensure that the rights and privileges and obligations of the English and French languages are respected on a constitutional basis. Part I and Part V, which deal with parliamentary procedure, legislative procedure and other procedure and other parliamentary instruments, with the administration of justice and also, in the same section, very clearly, in order not to leave any loophole in that legislation, that list a whole range-as others that 1 am now listing, communications and services to the public, working language-it is clearly understood that all this will naturally lead to a clear, outright and final expression, that the principles put forward in Sections 16 to 20 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms are completely respected, both in English and in French.

However, Mr. Speaker, we must remember that all amendments to the Charter of Rights and Freedoms which apply to federal institutions require the consent of Parliament and of the ten provincial legislatures. It goes to show how serious this is. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, all these rights are already deeply anchored in the constitutional rights set forth in the Official Languages Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 18,
I put a question to the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin), asking him what action he would take with regard to the overcharges placed by the banks on farmers across Canada in the early 1980s. I asked this question specifically because a number of farmers have found that they have been charged exorbitant amounts of interest over and above that to which they agreed on the original notes they signed when the banks switched fixed-rate notes to floating-interest-rate notes.
Several such cases have already gone to court and rulings have been made in favour of the farmers. In some cases, out-of-court settlements have been made involving hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Many months ago, in the early spring, the Minister referred the matter to the Inspector General of Banks, who is now the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, and I understand that that report was made available to him in late June. So far, the Minister has not made the report of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions available to the House. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will do that this afternoon on his behalf.
The other issue at stake is that a number of farmers who believe they have overpaid hundreds of thousands of dollars in interest have gone to their banks to receive copies of their liability ledgers or lists of notes they signed in the early 1980s. Before 1982, it was the practice of most banks to use a fixed-interest-rate-note form when lending money to farmers, and in fact, those are the legal documents and the ones that are binding in court. However, when some farmers have asked their bankers for copies of their liability ledgers, they have been told that they must pay as much as $500 just to see their documents.
I find it incredible that a bank doing business with a valued customer, business in many cases involving tens and hundreds of thousands of dollars and large interest payments, would not want to make those documents readily available. In any case, the banks are not making them available and many farmers are having difficulty proving their cases.
The House of Commons Agriculture Committee heard testimony from a lawyer who does a lot of business with farmers in southwestern Ontario, Mr. Larry Rider. He indicated that it was a very common practice for banks to switch from a fixed rate of interest to a floating rate of interest during the recession when interest rates were climbing dramatically. He said that he was sure that many farmers had paid exorbitant amounts of interest. Earlier I referred to two such cases. One was a court case in which some $250,000-worth of interest was awarded to the farmer. In another case in Alberta, some $240,000 was returned to the farmer in an out-of-court settlement.

August 24, 1987
Adjournment Debate
I believe the Minister of State for Finance should call the bankers and major financial institutions to ask them to make these documents freely available to their valued customers, including farmers and some small businessmen, so that they can handle their cases in an open, direct, honest and aboveboard manner. This matter is of national significance because tens of millions of dollars of interest payments are at stake.
It seems to me that unless the Government releases the documents of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and clarifies exactly where this whole matter is going, it should appoint a royal commission of inquiry to deal with this matter which affects many, many farmers and small businessmen who may have been overcharged large amounts of money.

It is very difficult for a farmer, unless he is extremely well off, to sue the bank because of the legal costs involved. As well, there is the danger of his credit being cut off. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since we were just talking about official languages I will be pleased, as a matter of courtesy, to answer the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) in his own language.

This issue of overcharging farmers by banks has been raised in this House on several occasions and has also been the subject of considerable public debate and attention in recent months. The debate centres on the past practice of chartered banks and other financial institutions relating to the past administration of their past floating rate loan portfolios. The proposition has been put forward that interest in excess of rates set out in loan documentation, signed by farmers and other businessmen, was illegally charged by banks to their customers. These claims arise from a long established administrative practice formerly engaged in by banks until their loan documentation was revised in the seventies and the early eighties. The practice consisted of documenting loans carried on a floating or variable rate basis through fixed rate demand promissory notes. That is, a customer who borrowed on this basis would execute a promissory note at the then prevailing interest rate and would be asked to sign new notes as rates changed. Over time, many banks ceased having new notes signed, for administrative ease, but notified clients of the new effective interest rates.
The banks no longer document floating rate notes on this basis but have developed and introduced floating rate promissory notes. It is understandable that the former practice might lead to confusion on the part of the borrower as to the interest
due on his loan. That is, is the floating rate or the fixed rate applicable? The issue in alleged cases of overcharging is whether the borrower knew and had agreed to the rates he was being charged. This is basically a legal question that raises issues of interpretation of the arrangements or contracts between the borrower and the lender. The proper forum for the resolution of disputes of this nature, which the Government has been saying all along, is the court system. Only a judge has authority to weigh evidence in a particular case, find facts, and order proper redress. The Government cannot act in the place of the judiciary, and only the judiciary can determine whether in a given case a farmer or other customer was overcharged or not.

Mr. Speaker, on August 19, 1987, I asked the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Cote) about the fate of the Native Economic Development Program. This program began in 1984 with a budget allocation of $345 million over a four-year period. It offered great hope to aboriginal groups that finally there was a serious commitment by the Government to advance the selfsufficiency of aboriginal communities and individuals by providing long term adequately funded business opportunities. In the first three and a half years, only 40 per cent of the funds were allocated. As I understand it, the program has been extended by one year to March, 1989. There then remains one and a half years to disburse the 60 per cent remainder of the committed funds.
The Minister answered my question by stating that a number of projects were being funded by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion. However, that was not my question.
Following the discovery two months into the fiscal year that the entire budget of the DRIE funds had been expended, a freeze was put on all DRIE and related programs, the Native Economic Development Program being one of those. It, of course, specifically addressed the needs of aboriginal communities. Although agreements signed with ministerial approval do seem to be honoured at the moment under the Native Economic Development Program, other applicants to this program are being told at one bureaucratic level that a freeze is on and at another that it is not. It appears that the serious mismanagement of the one program, DRIE, is resulting in the further mismanagement of another.
It is well known that over a century of colonial rule has destroyed the traditional land-based economy of Canadian aboriginal people. Aboriginal people are not asking for handouts. They are asking, and have been encouraged to ask, for assistance in developing small businesses which are relevant to many of the rural communities in aboriginal situations as well as assistance with financial institutions which will facilitate the
August 24, 1987

capitalization of such businesses when traditional lending institutions will not. They have received a mish-mash of programs operated by various ministries focusing on shortterm training and job creation and rarely resulting in enabling a stable, long-term economy to develop.
In fact, in the Government's own paper of July, 1987, entitled Consultation Paper on DRIE Native Economic Programs, they admit that to date the Government has been unsuccessful in addressing the economic needs of aboriginal communities. It says: "Efforts have resulted in only term employment at low wage levels".
The Native Economic Development Program offered at least one answer to this problem, but it now seems that aboriginal groups are the first to take the fall for the Government's admitted mismanagement of the DRIE program. The Government has offered promises and little money and now promises consultation and less money. Consultation is always useful, but not if it is simply another substitute for action.
In fact, in a briefing note to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) of July 23 it is indicated that on July 30 the Cabinet was to decide the future of native economic development programs, and this before a six-month consultation process with aboriginal people had even begun.
I dare say aboriginal people may be some of the most consulted people in Canada and have received some of the most apathetic action on their expressed concerns. It is no wonder that they have lost faith that their interests are being taken seriously by the Government.
We are talking here about people's lives, about whether the trapper, the fisher, the trucker, the store owner or the construction company can get started, hire people, and begin to address the extremely high rates of unemployment which exist in many aboriginal communities.
The House was recently told by the Government that the Canadian economy is doing pretty well, that jobs have been created. My question is simply oriented to ensuring that aboriginal people share in this. We cannot say that the Canadian economic situation has improved for all Canadians if a large segment of our population is left out. It is time for the Government to give some straight answers to aboriginal people.
My questions were really quite simple. While the Minister did confirm on August 19 that projects are being approved, I do understand that $43 million is unexpended under the Native Economic Development Program in this fiscal year. 1 further understand that, given the audit on the Department, Treasury Board authority is required to expend this amount and that the matter will be brought before Treasury Board on September 15.
Will the Minister confirm this information? Will he undertake, on behalf of aboriginal people, to do his utmost to ensure that this year's full allocation for native economic
Adjournment Debate
development programs is secured in addition to ensuring that the $345 million for the Native Economic Development Program is spent according to a previous commitment made?

subtopic: MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-UPGRADING OF INFRASTRUCTURES- GOVERNMENT'S REJECTION OF REQUEST FOR FUNDS- GOVERNMENT POSITION-COST OF UPGRADING
MUNICIPAL AFFAIRS-UPGRADING OF INFRASTRUCTURES- GOVERNMENT'S REJECTION OF REQUEST FOR FUNDS- GOVERNMENT POSITION-COST OF UPGRADING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some months ago at its most recent meeting, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities, having had a study done on the state of the infrastructure of most of the municipalities, particularly the large municipalities in Canada, including the state of the roads, sewers, sidewalks and water supply, realized that these services were deteriorating at a tremendously rapid rate. Given the sharp increase in the numbers of people living in our cities, it was felt important to bring to the attention of the federal and provincial Governments what was happening and to propose a plan to deal with this situation before a crisis arose.
As I drive around the City of Winnipeg I see sewer breaks, roads which have collapsed, sidewalks with large holes. I am sure other Members of Parliament see the same in their cities so I understand the needs outlined by the Federation. Healthy municipal services contribute to a healthy economy. Good roads are essential for getting employees to work and products to market. Industry, which this Government says it wants to encourage, needs the water systems to keep working and machines to keep operating. Bridges and sidewalks are equally important for the movement of people and products.
Studies have been done which show very clearly that if we leave these things too long, the cost of repair becomes astronomical. It costs almost three times as much to repair these facilities after 25 years as it would be to repair them after 15 years.
The municipalities have, in most cases, deferred the necessary maintenance of their roads, bridges, sewers and water distribution systems not because they are unaware of the problem but because of economic pressure. The revenue from taxes, federal and provincial funding and municipal taxes, have been inadequate to do the work which should be done.

August 24, 1987
Adjournment Debate
It is estimated that what needs to be done would cost about $12 billion in the next five years. What is proposed is a threeway funding, a third paid by the municipalities themselves, a third paid by the provinces and a third paid by the federal government.
That is a lot of money, but it was pointed out that to a large extent this cost would be self-financed because it would provide 280,000 person-years of work. Jobs would be created and the cost would be recovered through increased taxes paid by these people, through lower unemployment insurance payments and lower social assistance costs.
It makes eminent sense to me, and the proposal received the support of the Leader of the New Democratic Party and the support of the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner). I was shocked when 1 asked questions of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) to hear their very quick rejection of this proposal. They say they are not interested subsidizing municipalities. I find that very strange since they are prepared to subsidize provincial government infrastructure. In the regional development plans which are agreed on between the federal Government and some of the provinces, there are subagreements to fund highways and other projects. The projects about which the municipalities have talked are just as important. 1 would like to give one illustration of what this means.
I express my amazement that the Minister of the Environment, who comes from Prince Edward Island, does not realize, or does not know, about the tremendous problem in cities such as Halifax and Dartmouth. There are 200,000 or more people in those cities. They simply dump their sewage into the harbour. His own Ministry has estimated that only 13 per cent to 14 per cent of all the sewage in Nova Scotia is treated. How can a Minister from Prince Edward Island be so blind, so callous and so uncaring about a situation which exists just a few miles from where he lives?
This is a problem which is of tremendous importance. I urge the Government to stop thinking about the balance sheet for the immediate present and to think about the long-range consequences of not taking action. I think that the proposal made by the Federation of Municipalities makes eminent sense. It would bring benefits to the municipalities, lower unemployment and reduce our costs for dealing with the unemployed. It is one which the federal Government should give careful, sympathetic and early consideration to rather than the kind of brusque brush-off it has given to it.

Mr. Speaker, we have the answer to that question, but first of all I would like to emphasize my interest for that subject, first as an engineer by profession, and second
for having represented the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) at the Federation of Canadian Municipalities.
I would like, Mr. Speaker, to comment briefly on the position of the Government regarding the financing of municipal water and sewer systems. As my colleagues would know very well, for some time now the Canadian Federation of Municipalities has been asking the federal Government to pay over the next five years one third of an outlay which might be as high as $15 billion to help finance the municipal infrastructure and its replacement. Nearly half this amount would be earmarked for improving water and sewer services.
In 1980 the previous administration abolished a program of assistance in this field when financial restraints raised the issue of federal assistance in a field of provincial and municipal jurisdiction. Although this is still the case, new evidence at the international level leads to believe that not only are such grants inadequate from a constitutional standpoint and somewhat financially ill-advised, but they also can prove to be ecologically irresponsible.
I should like to draw the attention of the House to a recent publication of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development concerning the rates for water services. During a two-year study the OECD Environment Committee gathered data from 24 permanent member countries and became a strong supporter of the principle that the user should pay the cost directly. Another one of their conclusions is that the adoption of this principle would produce highly acceptable results from an environmental point of view.
This Government, our Government, firmly believes that the most viable and the most valid long-term solution to the many water problems in Canada lies in realistic rates, both in the literal sense, which means charging an adequate price for water used, and in a more general sense, and that is respecting the wide variety of values which water may represent and on which no rate can be set.
I also wish to mention a recent study of the American Waterworks Association which indicates that among the ten industrialized countries surveyed, Canada charges the lowest price to its industries. Canadian industry as a whole pays about one quarter the amount paid by the European industry for its water and about half the amount paid by our American neighbours.
You can be assured that the federal Government will assume fully the responsibilities conferred on it by our Constitution. However, it will promote the application of realistic guidelines for water; it will manage its own facilities and play a leadership role in the development of new techniques and the transfer of information; but it will certainly not propagate the idea of bad financial and environmental management by creating a national subsidy program in this area.
Mr. Speaker, this problem is completely outside our jurisdiction, and the proposal advanced as a possible solution is
